articles.title: White House doubles down after Trump angers base by floating illegal alien deal with Dems
articles.summary: Trump signaled willingness to work a deal for illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for over a decade, drawing fierce amnesty backlash.
articles.body:
The White House on Monday morning wouldn't rule out the administration working with Democrats on a "deal" for illegal immigrants who have been living in the U.S. for more than a decade as Republicans prepare to lose control of Congress in January.

President Donald Trump, in his first sit-down interview since sweeping GOP midterm losses, opened the door to the possibility of considering amnesty.

"The President never said the word amnesty," a White House official insisted to Fox News Digital.

"We want Democrats to show their cards," the official revealed.

They said, "There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump."

"Thanks to his efforts more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. and we have the most secure border in American history. Like the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to improve the lives of Americans and Make America Safe Again."

In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday, host Ross Douthat asked Trump how he is open to working with Democrats on immigration as he enters a lame-duck final stretch of his presidency.

"I'd love to do something on immigration," the president replied. "I think [immigration] both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law — that was that they came into the country illegally."

Trump, however, maintained that there are people in the United States who want to see all illegal aliens deported.

But, Trump said, "if they're good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases paying taxes, and there's a large group of people that think they should be allowed to stay."

"When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," he said, adding that people who he called "far-right" want deportations regardless of whether the illegal alien is working.

While Trump didn't say "amnesty," as the White House noted, he signaled in the interview his willingness to "work a deal" for people who have been in the United States illegally for "10 and 15 years" who haven't committed other crimes.

Rep. Maria Salazar, R-Fla., a longtime proponent of giving legal status to illegal aliens, celebrated Trump's comments on X.

"Well done, Mr. President! What you described on 60 Minutes is what the Dignity Act is all about," she said in the post.

Salazar's Dignity Act would offer legal status to people who have been in the United States continuously since 2020, provided they haven't committed other crimes and pay a restitution fee and back taxes.

The White House wouldn't clarify what such a deal could entail when asked Monday.

Notably, the interview was taped before Stephen Miller , a notorious immigration hawk, was selected to be Trump's new chief of staff.

Immigration restrictionism has been Trump's calling card since he first ran for president beginning in 2015. His comments in the interview that aired Sunday drew a sharp reaction from those favor immigration restriction.

"To be clear, if President Trump struck an amnesty deal with the Democrat-controlled Congress, it would be a bigger betrayal than starting the foolish war in Iran," commentator Steve Cortes said on X , adding a clip of Trump promising "the largest deportation operation in the history of our country" during a campaign rally in 2024.

"This plan absolutely guarantees that Texas never again votes Republican," said radio show host Anthony Cumia. "More states will turn permanently blue if illegals are given amnesty. Regan did the same this and California became a forever democrat state. Trump can do the same to Texas. Disgusting."

"Someone needs to tell Trump: Any amnesty deal with Democrats will destroy the Republican Party," said X personality Kelly McCarty. "We voted for NO amnesty and mass deportations of ALL illegals. No compromises. No exceptions."

articles.title: Doações: Lula recebe R$ 1,9 milhão e Flávio R$ 1 milhão após 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Repasses foram realizados do dia 26 de outubro até 9 de novembro; maior parte dos recursos enviados a Flávio são de empresários, enquanto Lula concentra doações da direção do PT e de financiamento coletivo.
articles.summary: Doações de campanha de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro após o segundo turno somam quase R$ 3 milhões, segundo dados do TSE. Lula soma R$1,9 mi, enquanto Flávio obteve R$ 1 mi
articles.body:
Presidente reeleito Lula e o candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Paulo Pinto e Joédson Alves/Agencia Brasil

A campanha do presidente Lula (PT), reeleito para o quarto mandato, recebeu quase R$ 1,9 milhão em doações desde o segundo turno da eleição, em 25 de outubro, segundo dados da prestação de contas no sistema do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). Já a campanha do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), derrotado por Lula, obteve cerca de R$ 1,1 milhão.

Os repasses foram realizados entre 26 de outubro e 9 de novembro. As informações estão disponíveis para consulta na plataforma Divulgacand, do TSE, em que os candidatos informam quanto suas campanhas gastaram e arrecadaram durante a disputa eleitoral.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, os dados da campanha de Lula estavam mais atualizados que os de Flávio. O petista relatou movimentações até 9 de novembro, enquanto a mais recente do senador foi no dia 4 deste mês.

A prestação de contas ainda é parcial. Candidatos que disputaram o segundo turno têm até o próximo sábado (14) para apresentar a relação completa de movimentações financeiras. Em paralelo, doadores podem continuar enviando recursos às campanhas dentro desse prazo. No entanto, empresas de financiamento coletivo (as chamadas vaquinhas) podem encerrar a arrecadação antes do fim do prazo, devido à necessidade de processar os pagamentos.

Márcio Nogueira, especialista em Direito Eleitoral e Digital e presidente da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil (OAB-RO), explica ao g1 que candidatos e partidos podem arrecadar recursos até o dia da eleição. Depois disso, a arrecadação só pode continuar em uma situação específica: para quitar despesas de campanha já realizadas, mas ainda não pagas. As dívidas, por sua vez, só podem ser contraídas até o dia das eleições.

🔎 Políticos que disputam eleições no Brasil não podem receber doações de empresas. As campanhas são financiadas com dinheiro público, por meio de repasses dos fundos partidário e eleitoral, e por doações de pessoas físicas, que podem mandar dinheiro diretamente ou por meio de plataformas de financiamento coletivo. Além disso, o candidato pode colocar dinheiro do próprio bolso. As campanhas são obrigadas a informar ao TSE os recursos que entram e também os que saem, com a contratação de serviços.

Enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro recebe mais recursos de empresários, a maior parte dos aportes para a campanha de Lula partiu do próprio partido e de financiamento coletivo.

Os partidos recebem dinheiro público por meio dos fundos e podem usá-lo para bancar as campanhas de seus candidatos.

O PT, além disso, tem pedido a filiados e apoiadores doações de R$ 13 para a vaquinha da campanha até 11 de novembro, último dia em que a conta do financiamento coletivo estará aberta.

O objetivo, segundo o partido, é ajudar a quitar as despesas da campanha. O PT afirma que a meta é arrecadar R$ 7 milhões até o dia 11. A título de comparação, a maior vaquinha eleitoral foi a do candidato à Presidência Renan Santos (Missão), que recebeu R$ 2,5 milhões de 15 de maio até 3 de outubro.

Do valor de R$ 1,9 milhão recebido pela campanha de Lula após a eleição, R$ 1,2 milhão foi pago pela direção nacional do PT. Outros R$ 746 mil saíram de financiamento coletivo. Dados do Divulgacand mostram que o presidente recebeu pelo menos 890 doações de R$ 13 em novembro, totalizando R$ 11,5 mil. A campanha também registrou repasses de outros valores que vão de R$ 1,86 a R$ 2 mil. Somente no dia 6 de novembro, foram 915 lançamentos, que somam R$ 26 mil.

Na campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro, a maior parcela das doações feitas nas últimas semanas partiu do empresário baiano Marcelo Soares Cruz, dono da Genesis Inovações Empresariais, que enviou R$ 585 mil. Soares Cruz foi o maior financiador individual da candidatura do senador, com repasses que somaram ao todo R$ 2,42 milhões. Conforme as regras do TSE, doações em dinheiro são limitadas a 10% dos rendimentos brutos do doador no ano anterior à eleição.

Outro doador de Flávio após a derrota do candidato do PL foi o arquiteto Julio José Franco Neves, que enviou R$ 300 mil. Ele havia depositado R$ 350 mil dois dias antes do segundo turno. Neves presidiu o Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand (MASP) durante 14 anos e é presidente de honra do museu.

O próprio candidato, que fugiu do Brasil no dia 27, doou R$ 11 mil para a sua campanha antes de ter sido derrotado por Lula, conforme os registros no TSE. R$ 5 mil foram enviados no dia 26, e o restante, no dia 29 de outubro.

Além disso, R$ 199 mil vieram do financiamento coletivo em sua vaquinha eleitoral. Outras 19 pessoas fizeram repasses ao candidato em valores que vão de R$ 0,01 a R$ 1.000.

Valores reportados pelas campanhas até agora

Ainda segundo o Divulgacand, a campanha de Lula soma R$ 132 milhões em receitas, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro declarou R$ 115,7 milhões.

Quanto ao total de despesas, a campanha de Lula declarou, até agora, ter gastado R$ 93,8 milhões. Ao mesmo tempo, a de Flávio Bolsonaro reportou gasto de R$ 114,7 milhões. Assim como no caso das receitas das candidaturas, as despesas ainda não são finais — o prazo para declaração ao TSE é o mesmo (14 de novembro).

A cada eleição, o TSE fixa um teto de gastos para cada cargo em disputa. Para os candidatos a presidente, nas eleições de 2026, o limite máximo de gastos é de R$ 88,9 milhões no primeiro turno e R$ 44,5 milhões no segundo turno. Ou seja, o político que participar dos dois turnos da eleição presidencial pode gastar até R$ 133,4 milhões.

O que acontece se uma campanha fica devendo?

De acordo com Jonatas Moreth, advogado com atuação em direito público e eleitoral e conselheiro seccional da OAB/DF, o partido deve assumir as dívidas se um candidato tiver mais débitos do que arrecadações.

"Neste caso deverão ser apresentados, na prestação de contas a) acordo expressamente formalizado, com anuência dos credores; b) cronograma de pagamento com prazo de pagamento que não ultrapasse o prazo para prestação de contas da eleição subsequente; c) indicação da fonte de recurso que será utilizada para quitação da dívida", afirmou ao g1 .

Dessa forma, o partido do candidato passa a ser "responsável solidário" pelas dívidas e deverá prestar contas deste pagamento. Nesse acordo, a sigla também deve obedecer às restrições às despesas eleitorais, como a vedação de recebimento de doações de pessoas jurídicas e limites de doações das pessoas físicas.

Em casos mais extremos e improváveis, se o partido não assumir a dívida ou se a prestação de contas for rejeitada por causa de irregularidades nos débitos, o candidato pode ter as contas julgadas como não prestadas ou desaprovadas. Isso pode resultar na perda da certidão de quitação eleitoral, impedindo o político de se candidatar em eleições futuras (inelegibilidade).

articles.title: Justiça Federal desiste de R$ 208,9 milhões extras para penduricalhos | G1
articles.standfirst: Luis Felipe Salomão, presidente do CJF, informou à AGU que novas fontes de receitas e ajustes de fim de ano permitiram cobrir as contas sem a necessidade de recursos adicionais.
articles.summary: A Justiça Federal desistiu do pedido de R$ 208,9 milhões extras para penduricalhos após identificar sobras orçamentárias para custear os benefícios.
articles.body:
A Justiça Federal recuou nesta terça-feira (10) do pedido feito à Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) para tentar viabilizar um crédito extra de R$ 208,9 milhões para bancar o pagamento de benefícios decorrentes de decisões do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) sobre penduricalhos.

🔎 A expressão "penduricalho" é utilizada para se referir a verbas indenizatórias, gratificações e auxílios que são somados ao salário de servidores públicos. Essas gratificações servem para compensar gastos relacionados ao exercício da função ou ressarcir direitos não usufruídos.

Em ofício enviado à AGU, o presidente do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) e do Conselho da Justiça Federal (CJF), Luís Felipe Salomão, informou que surgiram novas fontes de receitas e adequações orçamentárias – que são típicas desta época de final de ano com empenhos (valores reservados para as despesas) e despesas não efetuadas – o que provocou uma reanálise das contas.

Com isso, segundo o magistrado, a Justiça Federal vai conseguir pagar as contas sem necessidade de recursos adicionais.

No documento encaminhado ao advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias , Salomão solicitou que a AGU informe, aos relatores no STF de ações que tratam de pagamentos acima do teto constitucional, sobre a "desistência do pedido no que se refere ao Conselho da Justiça Federal".

O recuo ocorre um dia após a divulgação de reportagens que informaram que o CJF e a Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) haviam solicitado, em conjunto, cerca de R$ 533 milhões extras ao governo federal para viabilizar as despesas.

Enquanto a Justiça Federal estimava um impacto de R$ 208,9 milhões, o Ministério Público da União (MPU) apontou a necessidade de R$ 324 milhões para 2026.

Na ocasião, a AGU havia acionado o Supremo Tribunal Federal para que a Corte esclarecesse como as decisões sobre penduricalhos deveriam ser executadas diante do argumento inicial dos órgãos de que faltavam recursos no Orçamento.

A disputa orçamentária decorre de decisões do STF que autorizaram o pagamento da Parcela de Valorização por Tempo de Antiguidade na Carreira (PVTAC) para membros da magistratura e do Ministério Público.

A parcela equivale a 5% do subsídio a cada cinco anos de efetivo exercício jurídico, com limite máximo de 35%. Além da PVTAC, a Corte também autorizou a quitação de indenizações como férias e licenças-prêmio acumuladas por interesse público e auxílio-saúde mediante reembolso.

Inicialmente, o CJF havia argumentado que a suplementação era indispensável para honrar os pagamentos sem comprometer o funcionamento da Justiça Federal, sugerindo a edição de uma medida provisória com crédito extraordinário.

A consultoria jurídica do Ministério do Planejamento, contudo, apontou que despesas judiciais por si sós não preenchem os requisitos constitucionais de imprevisibilidade e urgência para a abertura desse tipo de crédito, o que levou a demanda para intermediação da AGU no STF.

Com a reavaliação orçamentária do CJF e a localização de sobras e receitas de fim de ano, a demanda da Justiça Federal foi cancelada. O pedido referente ao Ministério Público da União, no valor de R$ 324 milhões, permanece sob a análise provocada pela AGU junto ao Supremo.

articles.title: Boebert says ‘fat lady hasn’t sung yet’ in her House race
articles.summary: Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert (R) insisted Monday that her reelection race wasn’t over yet, despite CNN projecting a win for her Democratic opponent earlier in the day. “The fat lady ain’t sung yet,” Boebert told TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman near the House steps. “We have thousands of ballots that are being cured,” she continued, referring to…
articles.body:
Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert (R) insisted Monday that her reelection race wasn’t over yet, despite CNN projecting a win for her Democratic opponent earlier in the day.

“The fat lady ain’t sung yet,” Boebert told TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman near the House steps .

“We have thousands of ballots that are being cured,” she continued, referring to the process by which voters can correct errors on absentee or mail-in ballots.

The GOP lawmaker said this process would be completed Friday, following the Thursday evening correction deadline . Boebert also noted there are still military and overseas ballots that need to be received and tallied.

“So there’s thousands of ballots, and if it changes the outcome, it changes the outcome, and if not, we’ll accept the decision,” she told Wasserman.

The race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District is one of the last House contests yet to be called by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), along with more than a dozen others .

Democrats already secured control of both chambers of Congress in last week’s midterm elections , but additional seats would bolster the party’s chances of securing their legislative priorities.

Boebert’s opponent, Eileen Laubacher, was leading by less than 1 point as of Monday evening, with 95 percent of the vote in, according to DDHQ. Laubacher, a retired U.S. Navy admiral, declared victory in a Monday statement shared on her campaign social media account.

“This victory is historic,” the Democrat wrote in a post on the social platform X . “But making history means nothing if we don’t make a difference. My focus is simple: lower costs, protect healthcare, strengthen rural communities, take on corruption in both parties and hold Washington accountable.”

When pressed by Wasserman on Monday evening about how she would feel about losing her House seat, Boebert replied, “It’s almost liberating in a sense.”

“I want to offer condolences to some of my friends that did win,” she added.

The Colorado Republican stressed that she would want to ensure her staff had good placements outside of her House office if she lost her reelection.

“That would be a big priority. Other than that, this job doesn’t define me,” she told Wasserman. “Elections matter, but this doesn’t change who I am and what I do.”

articles.title: Conservative-leaning ballot measures win big amid GOP losses
articles.summary: Republicans are mostly grappling with the reality that many of their candidates lost, and some lost badly, in last week’s midterm rout. But amid the ruins they’ve also found a silver lining: across a smattering of states, voters approved ballot measures that affirm conservative views — including bans on transgender athletes in girls and women’s…
articles.body:
Republicans are mostly grappling with the reality that many of their candidates lost, and some lost badly, in last week’s midterm rout. But amid the ruins they’ve also found a silver lining: across a smattering of states, voters approved ballot measures that affirm conservative views — including bans on transgender athletes in girls and women’s sports — and rejected some progressive initiatives, like one in California that would have imposed a tax on billionaires.

That pulse check on the American people, even in states where Democratic candidates won big, could be the basis of the new conservative movement that will emerge from the electoral wreckage.

“In case you think the country went mad based on the results of the midterm elections, think again,” wrote the editorial board of the Washington Times last week. “The outcome of ballot measures across the country showed that common sense endures.”

In Washington state, voters approved a measure requiring schools and nonprofits to prohibit “biologically male” students from competing with and against “biologically female” students in sports. In Colorado, a narrow majority of voters agreed to “require all K-12 and collegiate sports to be separated based on biological sex,” with the exception of co-ed teams. Colorado voters also approved a prohibition on health care professionals providing surgeries to minors for “treatment in response to a minor’s perception of sex or gender.”

Voters in Arizona extended existing bans on transgender girls participating in girls’ sports, and in Nebraska, voters added a similar prohibition to the state Constitution.

It’s a striking rebuke of liberal views about sex and gender even in states that elected Democrats across the board. Conservatives are looking to those insights as a foundation for rebuilding a Republican Party based on their principles.

Akash Chougule , president of the Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity, a free-enterprise focused think tank, said the success of these ballot measures shows voters aren’t satisfied with what either party has done on certain social and cultural issues, which presents Republicans with the opportunity to reclaim that mantle as their own.

“One of the follies of the so-called ‘new right’ has been that they’ve successfully used culture issues as a political weapon, but they haven’t actually solved any of them. What we need is a constructive, conservative agenda that is clear about where we stand on these cultural questions and that has solutions to them that are still grounded in limited government,” Chougule said.

Other conservatives say it’s a chance to hold Democratic lawmakers accountable if they try to reverse the voters’ decisions. Terry Schilling , president of American Principles Project, said that while the ballot measures are good in the short term at reinforcing voters’ consensus on these social issues, he’s worried lawmakers in blue states will try to fight the referenda.

Fueling those concerns, Washington state Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad signaled in a statement last week that her party was interested in fighting the ballot measure results.

“The fight over I-638 is just beginning,” Conrad said, referring to the measure that prohibits biological men from women’s sports and requires sex verification. “We believe this initiative is unconstitutional on its face and support organizations planning to challenge it in court.”

Schilling also said Republicans should welcome any opportunity to get Democrats to vote for or against overturning or otherwise altering the policies created by the ballot measures’ success. That, he said, might expose Democrats as being out of touch with the voters in their own state.

“They all kept it pretty much, you know, ‘I don’t support men in girls’ sports,’ and so they gave the voters the impression that they’ll vote that way,” Schilling said of newly elected Democrats who campaigned on moderate social opinions.

“So now, as a Republican, you’ve got to be thinking to yourself: How do I expose them? How do I put as much pressure on them as possible? I would be bringing up these types of votes left and right, so that you get them on the record to show the voters almost immediately that they didn’t mean anything of what they said.”

Doreen Denny, senior advisor for Concerned Women for America Legislative Action Committee, said she was “not surprised in the least” by the ballot measure results, and that Republicans should take this chance to advance related policies, as should Democrats.

“Sex-based sports and spaces will continue to be a winning issue for the GOP,” Denny said. “Democrats ignore this at their peril. Many Democrats in red states ran against the party line for this reason… We hope the Dems see this moment as an opportunity to pivot from their losing position of rejecting fundamental rights for women and join Republicans in passing measures to protect women on the basis of sex.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

VIRGINIA ABORTION BALLOT MEASURE FACES LEGAL CHALLENGE

On the flip side, Virginia voters last week approved a ballot measure making abortion legal through the third trimester of a pregnancy, enshrining current protections into the state constitution in line with what the House of Delegates approved in 2025 and 2026. But that referendum is facing a legal challenge as anti-abortion groups argue the state skipped procedural steps in putting the measure on the ballot and misled voters.

Founding Freedoms Law Center, the legal arm of The Family Foundation in Virginia, is representing the Association of American Physicians and Surgeons and the Virginia Medical Freedom Alliance, both conservative medical advocacy groups, in suing to invalidate the ballot question.

They’re arguing that the language on the ballot hid the intent of the amendment that it was codifying and thereby confused voters into voting yes.

“We would just argue that when the people become the lawmakers, they need clarity on what the law will be,” said Victoria Cobb , president of The Family Foundation. “The ballot asked essentially whether to protect the freedom to make personal decisions, and then listed a bunch of things. The amendment creates a fundamental right to reproductive freedom.”

The question, as it appeared on the ballot, read like this: “Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) protect the freedom to make personal decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management, and fertility care; (ii) protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions; and (iii) allow for restrictions on access to abortion during the third trimester of pregnancy except when the patient’s health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive?”

It passed with over 62 percent of the vote. Cobb says she’s heard from voters who saw the third provision and voted yes, intending to back the third-trimester restrictions, and are now disappointed.

“So there were people who went to the ballot intending to vote in a, we’ll call it a pro-life manner, saw that it was about third trimester — allowing third trimester restrictions — and got confused and voted for creating a fundamental right to abortion,” Cobb said.

The measure’s success also strengthens their case, the opponents contend, because the plaintiffs can argue the damage of the language was that the law will be affected.

The parties will make their arguments in the Tazewell County Circuit Court on November 24.

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS GRUMBLE ABOUT STEPHEN MILLER

As Republicans return to a lame-duck Congress this week, some are already up in arms about President Trump’s latest high-profile personnel shakeup: the switch from Susie Wiles to Stephen Miller as White House Chief of Staff.

Some Republicans don’t think such a promotion is in order after Republicans’ midterm drubbing. Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) on Sunday suggested that Miller should have been fired instead.

“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” Stutzman said in an interview on CNN. “You don’t promote those who are — who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered.”

Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) also had harsh words for Miller on CNN. The two have clashed repeatedly over Miller’s push for hardline immigration policy.

“The worst of all possible choices,” Tillis told CNN’s Jake Tapper of Miller’s promotion. “The president needs to rethink it.”

Miller’s elevation signals that Trump is preparing to go to battle with Democrats when they retake the congressional majority, try to scale back the president’s deportation surge and pursue investigations against the administration.

“Stephen is a good choice on many levels, but face it, if the president was looking to build bridges with the new incoming Democrat majorities, he would probably have gone in a different direction,” former chief of staff Mick Mulvaney told my colleague Julia Manchester .

Although Trump has said he’s willing to work with Democrats in their new majority, promoting Miller also elevates a senior aide whom Democrats loathe and who is likely to dial in on executive authority before Trump’s term is up.

“They are not going to slow down on executive power, executive orders, and regulations,” said Joe Grogan , former director of Trump’s Domestic Policy Council in his first administration and senior adviser at Covington & Burling LLP. “Stephen is going to move aggressively on all of that.”

There’s a new conservative organization in town, and they’re narrowing in on promoting a new generation of Republican leadership ahead of 2028. articles.title: The worst possible man for the most important job
articles.summary: President Trump appointed Stephen Miller as white house chief of staff following the midterm elections, a move critics argue ignores voter rejection of his administration’s immigration policies.
articles.body:
After the blue tsunami swept the country on Nov. 3, everybody wondered how President Trump would respond. Would he get the message and tone down his rhetoric? Would he agree to work with Democrats to lower prices? Would he end the war in Iran, stop mass deportations, rein in ICE, and end other hardline policies that voters had just so soundly rejected? In other words, in the next two years, would we see a “kinder, gentler” Trump?

We soon knew the answer. The very next day, Trump climbed onto the roof of the White House and flipped America the bird.

No, of course, he didn’t literally do that. But he did something just as bad: He named Stephen Miller the new White House chief of staff. He could not have made a worse decision.

Granted, the president can appoint anybody he wants as his own chief of staff. We’ve seen some great ones in our day, among whom I would include James Baker, Howard Baker , Mack McLarty , Leon Panetta , Andy Card, John Podesta and Ron Klain.

But Trump’s nomination of Miller is not only wrong-headed but also dangerous. I say this for two reasons: for what it says about Trump, and for what it says about Miller.

What it says about Trump is that he has totally lost touch with the American people. Of several factors contributing to the lopsided results of last week’s midterms, there’s no doubt that one of them was public disapproval of mass deportations conducted by ICE and Customs and Border Protection, under policies developed by Miller.

From January 2025 to July 2026, 643 ,000 persons had been deported from the U.S. — about 25,000 of them to countries to which they had no connection. According to the Migration Policy Institute, 457,000 of these had no criminal convictions. Of those deported from the interior of the U.S. during that period, 2 2 0,000 had lived here at least two years , and 57,000 for at least 10 years, without any criminal record.

Americans recoiled at that wholesale anti-immigration crusade. That’s not what we voted for, they said. And in red states and blue, they expressed their opposition. Fifty-eight percent of those who voted on Nov. 3 said Trump’s deportation crackdown had “gone too far.” They were led by Americans aged 18-29, who shifted their allegiance from 2024 to 2026, Republican to Democrat, by 33 percentage points . Disaffected Latinos moved from Republican to Democrat by 28 points .

Trump doesn’t get it. On the one hand, he told “60 Minutes” that maybe his deportation policy was “too tough.” On the other hand, he doubled down, giving the chief architect of that mass deportation policy the most important job in his administration.

Miller seems driven by a hatred of immigrants, telling Fox News in 2023: “ We are being conquered .” Starting in Trump’s first term, he championed a zero-tolerance strategy that separated children from parents apprehended at the border. He convinced Trump to try to end “birthright citizenship.” He advocated suspending habeas corpus, closing the border to asylum seekers, and cutting back on new green cards . Under his direction, the Department of Homeland Security ordered ICE to make 3,000 arrests a day in order to deport a million immigrants in the first year of Trump’s second term. He called nurse Alex Pretti, shot and killed by ICE agents in Minneapolis, a “domestic terrorist” and a “would-be assassin.”

Which tells you all you need to know about Miller as chief of staff. No one could be more unqualified for the job. I once served as chief of staff to a California Republican state senator, and I can tell you that the position is a demanding one. You’re responsible for everyone your boss meets with, everywhere he goes, every piece of paper he sees, every decision he has to make or what decisions others can make for him. Perhaps, most importantly, you have to be honest enough to tell your boss when he’s dead wrong and when it’s time to change course.

Can you imagine Miller ever telling Trump he’s wrong about anything? No way. He’s a total sycophant. He’s more of a zealot than Trump is, as he proved again last Saturday at Mar-a-Lago. In his first speech since being named chief of staff, Miller pledged his “absolute loyalty” to Donald Trump and claimed that Trump had made the Republican Party “ stronger and more popular and more resilient than ever before .” This, after Republicans lost at least 45 seats in the House and seven seats in the Senate.

By naming Miller chief of staff, Trump has declared he’s not backing down on anything. It’s as if Nov. 3 never happened. God save the republic.

articles.title: Scott, Hawley decline to commit to backing Thune for leader
articles.summary: Two prominent Senate conservatives, Senate Steering Committee Chair Rick Scott (R-Fla.) and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), on Monday declined to commit to voting for Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) as Senate GOP leader after the party lost at least seven Senate seats in the midterm election. Scott, who signed a letter requesting to postpone Tuesday’s Senate…
articles.body:
Two prominent Senate conservatives, Senate Steering Committee Chair Rick Scott (R-Fla.) and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), on Monday declined to commit to voting for Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) as Senate GOP leader after the party lost at least seven Senate seats in the midterm election.

Scott, who signed a letter requesting to postpone Tuesday’s Senate Republican leadership election, said GOP colleagues need to define their goals before electing a leader.

“The first step is, one, what do we want to accomplish? And then anybody, including John Thune, if they want to be [leader], the first thing they have to say is: Do they want to do that?” Scott told Fox News Digital in an interview.

“If that’s not what they want to accomplish, then why would we elect them? If that’s what they want to accomplish, then tell us why they’re the best at it,” Scott said, explaining why he supported calls to delay the leadership election.

Scott said the timing of the leadership election should be based on how long it takes for Senate Republicans to define their goals for the lame-duck session and the next Congress.

“How long does that take? I think the first step is how long is it going to take us to agree on what our path should be. If we can get that done quickly, we can have elections after that,” he said.

Scott and four other Republican senators signed a letter spearheaded by Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) calling for a delay of Tuesday’s Senate GOP leadership election so that the Republican conference can have a “robust discussion” of what went wrong in this year’s election and evaluate leadership strategies moving forward.

Johnson told the Washington Examiner on Monday that he would walk out of Tuesday’s leadership meeting in protest if Republican colleagues call for a quick vote to elect the leadership team for the next Congress.

“If you hold the election, I’ll leave the room,” Johnson declared. “I’m not going to participate in elections for leadership tomorrow.”

Hawley, a rising conservative star, also signaled some dissatisfaction with the Republican leadership team on Monday.

He declined to commit to supporting Thune before Tuesday’s meeting of the GOP conference.

“I’m not going to pledge my vote to leadership. I’ll tell you that,” Hawley told a group of reporters , including CNN’s Manu Raju.

Sens. Mike Lee (R-Utah), Ted Budd (R-N.C.) and John Kennedy (R-La.) also signed the letter demanding a delay of the leadership election.

“Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice. It is certainly not the way leadership elections should be conducted in the world’s greatest deliberative body,” they wrote in a letter Monday to Senate GOP conference Chairman Tom Cotton (R-Ark.).

articles.title: Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth calls US House impeachment effort a ‘farce’
articles.summary: Hegseth condemns impeachment resolution against him as ‘sabotage’, defending his actions and policy decisions.
articles.body:
During a news conference, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has condemned impeachment efforts against him as “sabotage”.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt,” he said on Tuesday, calling criticism of him and the war on Iran “policy disagreements”.

Republican US Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth on Monday over the war on Iran, strikes on purported drug boats and other alleged violations of United States laws.

“This is not patriotism, this is sabotage,” Hegseth said on Tuesday.

In a post on Truth Social after Hegseth spoke, US President Donald Trump defended Hegseth and his statements, saying he “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”

The House of Representatives is likely to take an initial vote on the impeachment effort Tuesday, a procedural vote on whether to debate the impeachment resolution.

Republican Mike Johnson, who leads the party’s majority in the House, said on Tuesday that he expected a vote on the impeachment would be defeated.

“I expect that we’re going to defeat that one way or the other, and we’ll get on with the business,” Johnson said. “The idea that you would impeach the secretary of war at a time of international conflict sends a terrible message to our enemies and our allies, and we are not going to play that game.”

Massie’s last attempt to introduce the impeachment resolution against Hegseth in September was thwarted by Johnson, who avoided a vote in the Republican-led Congress by sending lawmakers home early.

On Tuesday, Massie said it was clear Hegseth had broken the law in the case of not obtaining authorization from Congress for the Iran war, which is one of the accusations in his impeachment resolution.

“The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity. Operation Epic Fury has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it,” Massie wrote on X, referring to the Pentagon’s name for the war. “Hegseth is breaking the law. Not even debatable.”

Speaking at his first news conference at the Pentagon in nearly six months, Hegseth defended his role in military actions ordered by President Trump.

Hegseth compared military losses under his tenure with other historic conflicts, saying some 60,000 Americans were killed in the Vietnam War, and 37,000 in the Korean War, while only 18 had died during the US-Israel war against Iran.

He addressed several of the issues raised in the impeachment resolution against him, including the lawfulness of strikes on alleged drug boats and the abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

The strikes on purported drug boats, Hegseth said, had been necessary to protect the US against narcotraffickers, and each strike had saved “thousands of American lives”. Maduro, the former president of Venezuela, Hegseth said, “was not kidnapped; he was brought to justice”.

“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” Hegseth said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, when asked on Tuesday about the impeachment effort, also defended Hegseth, saying actions including the strikes on drug boats and the Iran war were in response to “imminent threats” to the US.

“The president of the United States is the commander in chief, and he has a right to defend this country and to address imminent threats that pose a threat to the United States, and he’s done so,” Rubio said.

Hegseth, Rubio added, had acted on “a direct order from the commander in chief, who in our constitution is empowered and trusted with the job of keeping Americans safe”.

Impeachment likely to proceed at some point

A majority in the House is needed to take such a step, which then sends the resolution to the Senate, where lawmakers conduct an inquiry akin to a trial that can result in removal from office if two-thirds of the body – 67 lawmakers – support a conviction.

Democratic leaders have said they would support an effort to impeach Hegseth. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, said over the weekend that he supported Hegseth’s impeachment.

“The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said.

The Democrats will have a majority in the House starting in January, when new representatives are sworn in after highly successful midterm elections that saw Republicans lose many seats. Democrats in the Senate, however, do not have enough votes on their own to actually remove Hegseth from office.

Although Democrats will hold the majority in the Senate, they are expected to have about 54 seats in the upper chamber of Congress – short of the 67 votes needed to convict and remove Hegseth.

Vice President JD Vance also defended Hegseth in a social media post on Tuesday, stating that the process of impeachment “has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking”.

“Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements,” said Vance. “Rather than use them, they’re going to try to impeach Pete Hegseth.”

Speaking on a podcast on Monday, Republican Senator Ted Cruz said it was only a matter of time before Hegseth would leave his job in some way.

“Either Hegseth is gonna step down, either he will resign voluntarily, or Trump will fire him,” Cruz said. “Or if that does not happen, I think it’s extremely likely, if not certain, that the House will impeach him, because on the face of it the votes are there.”

articles.title: Alito may suffer from Ruth Bader Ginsburg syndrome
articles.summary: If Alito wants to preserve his legacy for a generation, he needs to retire fast while the MAGA Republicans still hold the majority.
articles.body:
The arrogance of power knows no partisan or ideological boundaries.

Liberal icon Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg often likened herself to the great Justice Louis D. Brandeis. Brandeis served 22 years on the Supreme Court, retiring at age 82.

In the closing years of the Obama administration, prior to the 2016 election, Ginsburg might have resigned at age 82, paving the way for the appointment of another liberal justice who shared her judicial philosophy. Instead, although diagnosed with cancer, she chose to soldier on and died in office in September 2020 at age 87 after 27 years of service.

President Trump wasted no time appointing as her successor conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett, creating the present court’s 6-3 conservative supermajority.

Ginsburg had said in 2016 that she “can’t imagine what the country would be — with Donald Trump as our president,” calling Trump a “faker.” She later said she regretted her remarks.

Justice Samuel Alito, now 76 , may well suffer from Ginsburg syndrome. The new Senate, with its decisive Democratic majority, is unlikely to confirm a hard-right justice. But the new Senate will not be seated until January. If Alito wants to preserve his legacy for a generation, he needs to retire immediately while the MAGA Republicans still hold the majority.

But according to the New York Times, Alito has told friends he does not plan to step down before the end of the court’s term in June, even though Democrats will assume Senate control in January. Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week.

As recently as last month, the conservative Alito had rejected the idea that he would step down if Democrats took control of the Senate.

“I intend to stick around through this term,” he told Bloomberg News , last month.

Alito has been an obdurate thinker inflexibly voting to rubber-stamp Trump’s outsized bid for executive power and his policies that bump up against constitutional norms. If Alito fails to retire this month, Republicans will have probably missed their window of opportunity for Trump to name a fourth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

But the Democratic landslide last week generated speculation that Alito or 78-year-old Justice Clarence Thomas — the court’s two oldest justices — could quickly announce their retirements and give Trump a shot at ramming through successors during the Senate’s lame-duck session.

Thomas has ruled out retiring, suggesting he might serve for decades more . With 35 years on the bench, if he were to stay through May 2028, he would already set the record as the longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history.

Despite the speculation, legal experts largely agreed after Election Day that fast-track retirements would not guarantee confirmation of a successor. The Republicans hold a majority in the present Senate of 53-47 . But a nominee would face the possible defection of departing Republican senators such as John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who were defeated in primaries by Trump-backed challengers.

In addition, there is Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a moderate who lost on Tuesday. She claims Justice Brett Kavanaugh misled her on overruling Roe v. Wade during his stormy confirmation hearing. And there is the maverick Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who may desert the fold. The group may have had little appetite to help Trump steamroll a nominee of his choice.

After Trump won reelection in 2024, the conservative legal analyst Ed Whelan said he expected Alito to announce his retirement the next spring and predicted Thomas would step down in 2026. The moves, he had believed, would allow Trump to replace the justices with younger jurists who might secure the court’s conservative supermajority for a generation. But no one likes to give up power voluntarily, irrespective of ideology.

But after Tuesday’s election, Whelan said the two conservative justices may not be able to retire before 2033 if they want to be succeeded by nominees with a similar judicial philosophy.

“No justice is going to announce in the next few days that he will be stepping down,” Whelan wrote , adding, “Justices don’t make snap decisions about retiring.”

Conservatives agonize that both men may follow Ginsburg’s unfortunate example. If a Democrat were elected to succeed Trump as president in 2028, both Alito and Thomas would be in their 80s before a Republican could regain the White House and be in position to nominate a successor.

In a series of interviews published in October, Alito acknowledged that he had “thought about” retiring at the end of the term, but said he had ruled it out, thinking he could “still make a valuable contribution.”

Meanwhile, a Democratic Congress will have other implications for the court. Recent polls show bipartisan support for enacting an enforcement mechanism for the ethics code the justices adopted in 2023, and for eliminating life tenure for justices.

Thomas, for example, could face renewed questions surrounding unreported gifts he accepted from his friend Harlan Crow, a Texas billionaire and Republican donor.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Ron Johnson threatens walkout of Senate GOP leadership election
articles.summary: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) pledged to walk out of the room if his Republican colleagues proceed with leadership elections on Tuesday, after calling a conference to discuss the party’s direction following significant losses for the GOP in the midterm elections. “If you hold the election, I’ll leave the room,” he told the Washington Examiner in…
articles.body:
Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) pledged to walk out of the room if his Republican colleagues proceed with leadership elections on Tuesday, after calling a conference to discuss the party’s direction following significant losses for the GOP in the midterm elections.

“If you hold the election, I’ll leave the room,” he told the Washington Examiner in a Monday interview. “I’m not going to participate in elections for leadership tomorrow.”

To delay internal elections, which are cast by secret ballot, Johnson will need support from a majority of the Senate GOP conference.

The Wisconsin Republican has been floated as a potential replacement for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) for when Democrats take control of the Senate in January, as some conservatives air frustration with Thune’s leadership .

Johnson, who has denied his interest in leadership in the past, again shot down the prospect on Monday, but he did not definitively rule it out.

“I don’t think so,” he told the Examiner. “It’s not my intention. I don’t want to be leader.”

The senator added that his request for a conference meeting was not a “hostile act” and was only intended to give the GOP the time to assess whether they wanted a change in leadership.

“We all like John Thune. We like him, OK?” Johnson said. “I don’t want to say anything bad about him, but again, at some point in time, our supporters absolutely believe we have to hold people accountable, and probably are looking for a new face, or new faces.”

Thune told reporters Monday he was anticipating a “very engaged conversation” at the Tuesday conference meeting.

“We’ll see where it goes from there, but, yeah, I’m running for leader, and I think it’s important that we have that discussion, and we will,” he said, according to Bloomberg .

No other Republican senator has publicly expressed interest in challenging Thune in a leadership contest. But others, including Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), have also pressed their GOP colleagues to delay the leadership vote.

Johnson also criticized President Trump’s midterm strategy in his Examiner interview, after Republicans lost key races in red states and control of both chambers of Congress in the election.

“I think there’s plenty of blame to go around,” he said. “But I mean, the president was the one out there saying, ‘Pretend I’m on the ballot,’ and people did, and we see the result.”

articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday that the effort to impeach him by an outgoing Republican congressman is nothing but a “political spectacle.”
articles.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday that the effort to impeach him by an outgoing Republican congressman is nothing but a “political spectacle.” “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said during a press conference at the Pentagon. He said the effort sends a dangerous message to America’s enemies around the world. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., reintroduced articles of impeachment Monday over the war with Iran and other military actions that were ordered by President Donald Trump. Hegseth likened the effort to Congress’ two failed impeachment trials against Trump during his first term — first over a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the second over the Jan. 6, 2021, attack at the U.S. Capitol. “Both times they failed, both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House,” Hegseth said. “Now they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his Cabinet. They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.” Trump weighed in on social media shortly after Hegseth finished, writing that the defense secretary “gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Hegseth painted a rosy picture of America’s standing in the Iran war. He defended his record as defense secretary as he listed his accomplishments over the war with Iran, operations in Latin America to go after alleged drug boats, and the military’s secret effort to nab Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Maduro and his wife are facing charges in the U.S. that they have denied. Trump called the Iran conflict a “minor incursion” that would last only four to six weeks. It has dragged on into its ninth month, U.S. munitions are depleted and the Republicans saw massive losses in the midterm elections over high gas prices, inflation and opposition to the Iran war. Republicans and Democrats in Congress have been frustrated by the amount and caliber of information Hegseth has provided them about the ballooning costs of the Iran conflict, which could be as high $100 billion, NBC news has reported. The Pentagon is still seeking a budget that has not yet been approved. Massie, a longtime Trump critic who’s retiring from Congress at the end of the year, brought eight charges against Hegseth, accusing him of “waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat.” His actions mean that House GOP leaders will be forced to bring the impeachment articles up for a floor vote within two legislative days because he filed the measure as privileged under House rules. A simple majority vote is required in the House for the articles to be approved. If the effort is successful, the resolution is then sent to the Senate to decide whether to convict and remove Hegseth from office. Republicans could also make a motion to kill the resolution, which would require a majority vote. “This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”

articles.title: If you want more babies, make remote work easier
articles.summary: Any right-thinking conservative who priorities fertility should prioritize facilitating remote work, because it raises the odds that couples turn plans into children without building a new entitlement state.
articles.body:
A toddler wanders into the frame as the morning standup starts, and the meeting still begins on time. The commute never happens. The pickup plan stays intact, and dinner becomes a given instead of a gamble.

That everyday relief has a demographic edge. A new paper on working from home and fertility links remote access to higher realized and higher planned fertility across the U.S. and dozens of other countries. For an administration that says it wants more children , the cheapest, most scalable lever sits inside the workweek.

Conservatives have elevated fertility into a core concern, arguing that low birthrates threaten social stability and long-run economic strength. The Institute for Family Studies has followed that rise through its coverage of the American pro-natalist moment . Yet political energy keeps drifting toward expensive, hard-to-administer fixes .

Remote work offers something rarer: a structural change that reduces the daily costs of childrearing without requiring a vast new benefits system.

That is why the Trump approach to remote work creates a sharp contradiction. Federal guidance in 2025 reinforced a push to bring workers back on site through a directive demanding a return-to-work in person . You can support managerial accountability and still recognize the tradeoff: when government models rigid office norms, it signals to employers and workers that flexibility is a luxury rather than a tool.

The “Work from Home and Fertility” paper puts numbers on what families have already sensed. The authors estimate that work-from-home policies accounts for 8.1 percent of U.S. fertility — about 291,000 births per year as of 2024. The authors also find bigger effects when both partners have work-from-home access: one flexible schedule helps, two flexible schedules change the whole household operating system.

The mechanism stays straightforward. Remote work returns time, and time drives family formation. A January 2026 revision of the National Bureau of Economic Research study “Why is fertility so low in high-income countries?” argues that modern low fertility reflects more than prices and paychecks. Remote work does not override every cause, but it removes friction that blocks second and third children: commuting hours, fragile pickup plans, and the career cliff that hits the parent who becomes the default logistics manager.

By contrast, conventional pronatalist policy usually means large public spending for modest gains. Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development countries spent an average 2.35 percent of GDP on family benefits in 2021, while the U.S. spent less than 1 percent of GDP, according to family benefits spending . Matching the European scale would mean a permanent fiscal expansion.

Even research that finds positive links between spending and fertility attaches them to big price tags, like the estimate that an extra 1 percent of GDP in early childhood programs associates with about 0.2 additional children per woman in early childhood spending.

Fertility treatment initiatives face the same budget reality. The Trump administration’s 2025 IVF order cites $12,000 to $25,000 per cycle. That cost structure makes broad coverage politically and fiscally contentious, even for leaders who sincerely want more births.

Remote work scales differently because it rides on existing employer budgets and modern digital infrastructure. Economists estimate that 37 percent of U.S. jobs can be done entirely at home , and evidence shows remote work has persisted well above pre-2019 norms. When feasible, flexibility also boosts retention, widens hiring pools and reduces commuting burdens, giving the policy benefits far beyond fertility.

Any right-thinking conservative who prioritizes fertility should prioritize facilitating remote work. It raises the odds that couples turn plans into children without requiring a new entitlement state.

articles.body:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) announced she intends to seek another term leading the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), the campaign arm for Senate Democrats, following sweeping victories across the country this year.

“I am definitely going to volunteer again,” Gillibrand told Nexstar Media Group Washington correspondent Margaret Chadbourn in an interview. “I think we can build on our success for next cycle.”

Democrats gained at least seven — but possibly up to nine — seats in the upper chamber last week, including big wins in deep red states like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. The party is hoping to add victories in Mississippi and Alaska to its tally.

The New York Democrat took over the role at the beginning of 2025.

Gillibrand said she predicted her party could win that many seats when she first took the job, back when the possibility of a Democratic majority, much less a sizable one, seemed unlikely. To win control of the Senate, Democrats needed to not only hold on to their own seats but defeat opponents in red and purple states won just two years ago by President Trump.

“A year and a half ago, I did say we could win between seven and nine seats,” Gillibrand said. “I knew that to create a blue wave, you need a few things … You need great candidates standing in red states ready to go, and you need a toxic climate led by a president who’s not listening to the American people. And I saw that coming.”

Gillibrand would need her New York partner, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, to reappoint her as DSCC chair. He has not yet said whether he will do so.

The DSCC chair is the primary person in charge of helping Democrats reach a majority in the gSenate, primarily by recruiting candidates and determining where party money is spent.

Even after massive gains, Gillibrand is eyeing more in 2028.

Democrats will have the chance to go for something they have not achieved since a brief period in 2009: 60 Senate seats, a filibuster-proof majority. If the party ends up with 56 seats after this election, they would need a net gain of four to reach that threshold.

Gillibrand specifically pointed to opportunities in North Carolina, Wisconsin, Iowa and possibly even Florida, where Democrats came up just short this cycle.

“I think there’s more states we can put in play,” Gillibrand said. “There’s a lot of opportunity next cycle that we can try to build on what we did this cycle.”

articles.title: Measure the crime, Alaska: Seizing a plane over a six-pack defies logic
articles.summary: Under such an evaluation, essentially no fine is ever excessive.
articles.body:
On the runway in Fairbanks, Ken Jouppi was loading his Cessna for a short hop to Beaver, Alaska , a village of a few dozen folks on the banks of the Yukon. His passenger was flying out to see her husband for her birthday, and she’d packed some beer in with the groceries.

Troopers showed up with a warrant before the plane ever left the ground.

Some of you might be thinking, yikes, is Jouppi another Andrew Carter Thornton II? “ Cocaine Bear ,” the sequel? Nope. Beaver’s a dry town. Not the weather, the beer. Bringing alcohol into Beaver’s a crime, and he and his passenger were both convicted of a misdemeanor. Three days in jail apiece and a $1,500 fine, as low as the law goes .

But then Alaska did something extraordinary: It took Jouppi’s plane.

Drive some liquor into a dry village, and Alaska will take your truck only if you’re a repeat offender or hauling serious quantities. Fly it in, first offense or not, and the airplane’s gone. Jouppi’s Cessna was worth about $95,000 , more than 60 times the fine the judge actually imposed. That was 2012. Jouppi is now in his 80s, still fighting for his plane, and on Dec. 1, the Supreme Court will finally hear him out .

You’d think nobody outside Fairbanks would care about this, right? But the taking of someone’s plane won’t stop at the Yukon. Locking someone up costs the government money. Yet fines are quite different. Justice Scalia called them “a source of revenue,” and forfeitures fill the same till. In 2023 , the federal government alone forfeited about $4.5 billion in property; the states chipped in close to another $300 million.

Justice Thomas has warned that these operations “frequently target the poor”. I don’t think Alaska’s trying to pay the bills and make up for a budgeting shortfall with Jouppi’s Cessna. Alcohol’s hit rural Alaska hard, and Beaver went dry after a young man in the village spent a night drinking, passed out in sub-zero cold, and choked to death .

While I’m not thrilled that the government attempted to seize Jouppi’s plane, there could be a myriad of reasons. But how the Alaska Supreme Court got to its answer upholding that is quite perplexing. The Alaska Supreme Court reasoned that the Alaska legislature determined that the harm from even a six-pack of beer knowingly imported into a dry village is severe enough to warrant forfeiture of an aircraft . To size up that harm, the court reached past the six-pack in Jouppi’s plane to the toll alcohol has taken across rural Alaska.

You can do that with just about any offense. Speeding kills thousands of Americans a year. Hold one driver doing 10 miles per hour over up against all of that, and the state could take his car easily. Under such an evaluation, essentially no fine is ever excessive, and any city that comes up short at budget time has its answer to every excessive-fines claim; the problem’s serious, so the penalty stands.

The idea behind the Eighth Amendment is a good deal older than the Constitution. At Runnymede in 1215, the barons got King John to promise that a free man would be fined “for a small fault only according to the measure thereof.” Later kings didn’t much care for that promise, and when Parliament drew up the English Bill of Rights in 1689, it declared that “ excessive fines ” ought not be imposed.

Virginia lifted that language nearly verbatim for its 1776 Declaration of Rights, and Virginia’s version became our Eighth Amendment . In 1799, Judge Paul Carrington, who had served on the committee that drafted that Declaration , wrote that nothing could be added to an offender’s punishment “beyond the real measure of his own offence.”

Measure the crime and fine against the man. Anything less is a chilling overreach of government power, and one that happens to line the government’s pockets. Three days in jail and a $1,500 fine fit what Jouppi did. When the justices take the bench on Dec. 1, I hope they tell Alaska that its position has been weighed, measured and found wanting .

Brian Daniel Mounce is a law professor at the University of Memphis.
