articles.title: GOP wipeout goes from bad to worse as Dems quietly score another major win with big ramifications
articles.summary: Democrats flipped legislative chambers in Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona and other battleground states, creating trifectas that could reshape redistricting.
articles.body: In addition to taking control of the House of Representatives, the Senate, and the majority of governorships on Tuesday, Democrats have also assumed control of the majority of state legislatures across the country for the first time in over a decade. Heading into the election, Republicans controlled 28 of the nation’s 49 bicameral state legislatures, compared with 18 controlled by Democrats, while three states had divided control. Democrats now control both chambers in 24 states, compared with 22 for Republicans. North Carolina and Texas have split legislatures, while races in Alaska and Georgia remain pending. Even if Republicans win the uncalled chambers in the pending states, Democrats will still control more state legislatures than Republicans. Nebraska is included in the Republican count because its officially nonpartisan, unicameral legislature is led by a Republican majority. Democrats scored major victories in several pivotal battleground states during the 2026 midterms, flipping legislative chambers and securing full control of state governments in places that will shape redistricting and election rules ahead of 2028. In Wisconsin, Democrats captured both the Assembly and Senate for the first time in years, pairing the wins with the governorship to create a trifecta. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Similar gains unfolded in Michigan, where the party flipped the House and expanded its Senate majority alongside a Democratic governor, and in Minnesota, where Democrats reclaimed the House, held the Senate, and won the governorship. Pennsylvania Democrats flipped the Senate while retaining the House, and Arizona voters handed Democrats majorities in both chambers. New Hampshire also saw Democrats flip both houses of the legislature, while the party picked up the House in Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas. The shift gives Democrats significantly more power to shape policy across the country as state lawmakers play a central role in setting election rules, drawing congressional maps, approving budgets and advancing laws on issues ranging from abortion and guns to education and labor. The change could also have major implications for redistricting. States will redraw congressional and legislative maps after the 2030 census, and the party controlling state government will have greater influence over how those districts are designed. Democratic control could also lead to legal battles over existing maps and efforts to alter election administration rules ahead of future presidential contests. HOUSE DEM WHO DEFIED HAKEEM JEFFRIES SCORES UPSET WIN IN PRO-TRUMP DISTRICT Democrats could similarly revive efforts to pass stricter gun laws, increase funding for public education and expand labor protections. Depending on the state, lawmakers could also target voting restrictions, expand access to mail-in and early voting, or change how elections are administered. Results confirming Democratic control of the majority of state legislatures come days after the party captured control of both chambers of Congress and the majority of governorships. Axios reports that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "In a historic victory, Democrats now hold more than half of the seats at the state legislative level nationwide," Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee President Heather Williams said in a press release. "These victories reinforce the DLCC’s national strategy to build power for Democrats all across the country. Whether competing for new majorities, breaking GOP supermajorities, or gaining seats to give Democrats more leverage to fight for their constituents, when these races have the resources they need, we can deliver wins in red, blue, and purple states alike." Additionally, Democrats may now have the necessary votes to move forward with the National Popular Vote plan, which would bypass the Electoral College, Fox News Digital reported on Sunday. The economy, government corruption, war in Iran and increasingly negative views of President Donald Trump's job performance created a perfect storm for Democrats, Fox News voter polling showed. Voters cast their ballots with a bleak view of the country in their minds. Three-quarters said they felt dissatisfied or angry about how things were going, while just a quarter were satisfied or enthusiastic. Three-quarters rated the economy negatively, a stark reversal from this point in Trump’s first term, when positive ratings outnumbered negative ones by 2-to-1, as shown in the 2018 Fox News Voter Analysis survey (66% positive, 34% negative).

articles.title: Dem governor’s tale of combat action torn to shreds by commanding Army officer: 'Give me a break'
articles.summary: Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore's former Army supervisor in Afghanistan says his claims of leading paratroopers in combat are "not truthful."
articles.body: Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, widely believed to be considering a presidential run in 2028, is facing renewed scrutiny over his resume — this time from his former Army supervisor who is questioning the governor's claim that he led soldiers in combat. In an investigative deep dive into Moore's military service, The Baltimore Sun spoke with a retired Army Lt. Col. James A. "Jamie" Gottschling, who served with Moore in Afghanistan in 2005 and 2006. What Gottschling described was Moore's patriotic service and dutiful fulfillment of his role, but exaggerations — and in some cases falsehoods — about incidents that occurred overseas. Moore's team said that "partisan politics got in the way" and led to Gottschling's latest assessment, where he told Fox News Digital: "I wouldn't call him a soldier." Fox News Digital spoke with Gottschling on Monday. WES MOORE PREEMPTIVELY UNLOADS ON BALTIMORE SUN AHEAD OF EXPOSE, AS SPOX BEEFS WITH 'RIGHT WING' OWNERSHIP He said in the interview that while Moore would occasionally leave the base, the governor never saw combat. Gottschling said he would describe Moore and himself as "combat veterans" who are "not veterans of combat." "When you think of a veteran of combat, you think somebody that's in a foxhole, getting shot at, IED blowing up the convoy, or even more dramatically, when you think about World War II movies, Easy Company, or any of those things where it's like, those guys are getting shot," Gottschling said. "That just wasn't the environment that he was in." "He starts talking about, you know, in his TED Talk and really struggling with reintegration into the civilian world after the deployment, I'm like, 'what is he talking about?' You know, he spent six months over there, basically in, you know, a forward base that pretty much is as safe as anywhere. You'd probably be at more risk going to an ER in any of the cities in the United States than you would be in Afghanistan, in Salerno." Moore is widely considered a contender for the 2028 Democratic Party nominee for president. "I just think it's disingenuous to really associate with the struggle. I mean you can have some empathy for people that might struggle with the transition, but when you come over there pretty much dip into a combat zone situation, work on the staff for six months and then come out you know saying that, you know, all this trauma that you had ... and it's like, oh, give me a break," Gottschling told Fox News Digital. "So I think it's just him emotionalizing and capitalizing on what soldiers do. And he's not a soldier," he continued. "He was in the Army as a reservist in a staff position in Iraq, but I wouldn't call him a soldier." The Baltimore Sun report describes Gottschling, who then held the rank of major, as the "Army officer who supervised Moore daily" in Afghanistan. Moore has framed himself as a paratrooper in the famed 82nd Airborne Division who led troops into battle during his deployment overseas. Moore worked on information operations coordination while the pair were stationed together at Forward Operating Base Salerno in the Khost Province near Afghanistan's border with Pakistan. According to The Baltimore Sun, Moore's job was "analyzing reports from infantry battalions and provincial reconstruction teams, coordinating for civilian assistance and helping Afghan officials communicate with the public." Central to Moore's personal narrative is that he led troops into combat in Afghanistan. He said that on multiple occasions on X while he was campaigning for Maryland's governorship. WES MOORE WARNS DHS FEDERAL OCCUPATION OF NEW ICE COMPOUND NOW UNDER STATE INVESTIGATION "I’ve seen real patriotism when I led paratroopers in combat in Afghanistan and I’ve seen it in my own family," he said in a Nov. 6, 2022 post, just two days before he was elected governor. "Service has defined my life, starting when I joined the Army when I was 17, through leading soldiers in combat with the 82nd Airborne in Afghanistan, to today," he said in a post earlier that year. In his book, "The Work," Moore describes being shot at. "As a soldier, you never forget the first time you were shot at," he wrote in the book. "A sudden, stunning commotion engulfs you—the sound of shells buzzing past your ears, a flurry of divots leaping out of the earth around your feet—but then your training kicks in," the book says. "Moments before those first shots came at me, I was convinced I was prepared for the experience," the book continues. MARYLAND'S LONE CONGRESSIONAL REPUBLICAN BLASTS MOORE'S REDISTRICTING PUSH AS ALLEGED 2028 WHITE HOUSE PLAY Moore, who is widely considered a contender for the Democratic nominee for president in 2028, reaffirmed that that passage from his book was true during a July interview with CNN, again claiming that he "led soldiers in combat." Gottschling also contests the extent to which Moore led other soldiers. In "The Work," Moore described fellow soldiers as "my paratroopers" and rejects Moore's framing that he was ever "leading" troops in combat. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moore's senior press secretary described Gottschling's motives as political. "Five days after Marylanders re-elected Governor Moore in a historic landslide, Sinclair is back to swiftboating a veteran by recycling the exact same stories and interviews they already ran months ago," Ammar Moussa said. "Twenty years ago, before partisan politics got in the way, Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling signed an official Army evaluation declaring Wes Moore a ‘top 1% officer’ and ‘the best lieutenant I've encountered during Operation Enduring Freedom.'" Gottschling addressed that evaluation with The Baltimore Sun. "There’s a lot of embellishment with that, but that’s just how the system was," he told the outlet. "You’re not trying to be deceitful about it, but you want to elevate what they did (your soldiers) … so they can get their next job or next promotion." "Now, a longtime Donald Trump donor who has openly stated his goal is to stop Governor Moore from being in contention for the presidency is working with Sinclair to contradict his own signed military records," Moussa continued. "Governor Moore’s service in Afghanistan—including earning the Combat Action Badge and coming under rocket fire alongside fellow service members—has been independently verified by official Army records and The Baltimore Banner, which interviewed fellow service members, and no partisan swiftboat campaign will change the facts." The Combat Action Badge is also addressed in The Baltimore Sun's story. The story describes it as a "minor indirect rocket attack" where nobody was injured. Moussa, citing a report in the Baltimore Banner, said a Marine named Anthony Del Signore who was attached to Moore's unit said that their convoy "took some shots" at least once. A New York Times exposé found in 2024 that Moore for years claimed to be the recipient of a Bronze Star when he had not been awarded one at the time. He included the Bronze Star claim on his resumé when applying for a White House fellowship in 2006. In 2024, he received the award after then-Sen. Laphonza Butler, D-Calif., urged the Army to give him one. In a story published in July on the topic of Moore's military service, Gottschling said he doesn't want Moore to be president. At that time, Moore was running for reelection as governor. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I care about my faith and country. I do not really care whether Moore is elected governor of Maryland, but I do care if he is in contention for the presidency," he said. "I could not live with myself if I was not vocal about the truth." Gottschling made it clear that he wasn't putting down Moore's service, which he called exemplary, but took issue with what Moore said about his service after he came home and elevated his political profile. Gottschling called Moore a "valued staff officer" and said he "appreciated every minute" of the work he did. "I think there's nothing wrong with that, if it ended there, that would be it," Gottschling said. "But it didn't end there. The embellishment, the aggrandizing of his actions over there that didn't take place is the problem that I have. I'm a pursuer of the truth, you know, and I want to tell the truth."

articles.title: Buttigieg challenges political status quo in new book ‘Next’
articles.summary: Pete Buttigieg — who has said he’s leaning toward a 2028 presidential run — is penning a book that he describes as focused on taking “big swings to reform our political system.” The former Transportation secretary announced the Jan. 26 release of his new book, “Next,” on Tuesday. The book, Buttigieg said in a video…
articles.body:
Pete Buttigieg — who has said he’s leaning toward a 2028 presidential run — is penning a book that he describes as focused on taking “big swings to reform our political system.”

The former Transportation secretary announced the Jan. 26 release of his new book, “Next,” on Tuesday.

The book, Buttigieg said in a video posted on Instagram, is “not a policy manual.”

“It’s an account of how we got here and an argument about what could happen if America takes big swings to reform our political system. If we do that, we can have a life that is better, not just better than today, but better than before,” Buttigieg, 44, said.

Simon Six and Avid Reader Press, trade divisions at publisher Simon & Schuster, said in his book the former mayor of South Bend, Ind., “makes the urgent case for seizing the current moment of political rupture as a chance to deliver transformative improvements that the majority of Americans demand” and “lays out a vision for addressing the profound challenges facing our country today.”

With the book, the publisher said, “no matter who the next American president will be, if you are reading ‘Next,’ you are holding our nation’s future in your hands.”

From then-Sen. Barack Obama (D-Ill.) in 2006 with “The Audacity of Hope,” to former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R) and Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) prior to their 2024 presidential runs, authoring a book has almost become a rite of passage for political candidates ahead of their White House bids.

Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic presidential candidate, said in an August interview on “The Diary of a CEO” that he was favoring another run for office in 2028.

“I think I’m more inclined than not, but there’s so much we don’t know,” he said at the time.

articles.title: The new Democratic Congress must work with Trump to win the Iran war
articles.summary: Congressional Democrats should not replace Trump’s hubris with their own — how the Iran hostilities are ended matters greatly.
articles.body:
For the last two years, President Trump has made the colossal mistake of misinterpreting his impressive re-election comeback in 2024 as a public mandate to do whatever he wanted to advance the national interest as he saw it, even as a form of self-aggrandizement. Without input from Congress or the judgement of some of his own national security advisers, he heeded only the advice that already matched his own instincts.

The success of his operation to seize dictator Nicolás Maduro from Venezuela in an efficient and casualty-free strike seemed to have convinced him that it could be replicated on a somewhat larger scale in Iran. The fact that the Iranian military and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were far more formidable than the Venezuelan army and police did not dissuade him from his quest.

The existence of a highly motivated and active civilian opposition in Iran was perhaps seen as a guarantee of victory — he needed only to call upon them to rise up, as they had during the Obama administration . Unlike Obama, he implied, he would respond with U.S military power. “Help is on its way,” he promised .

Unfortunately, there was no actual coordination or integration between the citizen uprising, the U.S. bombing campaign , and related military and information operations. As a monumentally tragic result, tens of thousands of defenseless protesters were killed by the regime as America stood by. The U.S.-caused debacle has severely damaged America’s credibility and made future cooperation with the Iranian people more difficult.

A major factor in the Democrats’ ascendancy in last week’s midterm elections was Trump’s erratic conduct in the Iran war and its negative impact on domestic energy prices and U.S. inflation. The growing opposition to Trump’s “war of choice” stems in large part from its dramatic contrast to his longstanding and vociferous opposition to “endless wars,” especially in the Mideast, and his pledge of “no new wars” across the board.

The knee-jerk reaction among most Democrats and some Republicans is to bring the war to an immediate end. But those who heed that call for humiliating retreat, which is how America’s enemies will see it, risk compounding Trump’s careless warmaking by their own rash actions — how the Iran hostilities are ended matters greatly.

If the U.S. walks away from the situation, leaving the aggressive Islamist regime in power, free to advance its nuclear ambitions, criminally oppress its population, and move aggressively against its neighbors and the U.S.-led international order, Trump or his successor will soon need to confront Iran’s threat all over again

Instead, Democrats should take advantage of the political interregnum and approach Trump now, proposing a cooperative, bipartisan plan to end the conflict with Iran by ending the regime that is its perennial cause. This plan will require reassuring and coordinating with the Iranian opposition and with America’s European and Mideast allies. With a minimum of kinetic action, the plan should rely on heavily increased economic pressure and on integrated special operations to conduct information warfare, support a mass civilian uprising and selectively arm elements within the population.

A U.S. president and a Congress newly unified and invigorated in the objective of peaceful regime change would greatly enhance the prospect of mass Iranian defections and the regime’s splintering and collapse.

Such bipartisan cooperation on regime change in Iran would remove all Iranian and U.S. constraints on the free flow of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz and eliminate a major cause of inflation and unaffordability. It would also augur well for presidential-congressional partnership on a range of issues, both foreign and domestic, over the next two years and redound to the lasting credit of all parties.

Finally, a Trump-Congress breakthrough would demonstrate the inherent self-correcting nature of democracy when the voices and votes of the people demand cooperation from their chosen leaders, out of the ashes of partisan division, bitterness and anger.

Rekindling the World War II spirit of bipartisan unity and democratic resilience would erase the virtual smirking of the authoritarian leaders in Iran, Communist China, North Korea and Russia, who prematurely celebrated the demise of America’s democratic model. And the Free World will surely welcome the return of unified American leadership.

Joseph Bosco served as China country director for the secretary of Defense from 2005 to 2006 and as Asia-Pacific director of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief from 2009 to 2010. He is a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Corean-American Studies, a member of the advisory board of the Global Taiwan Institute and member of the advisory board of the Vandenberg Coalition.

articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) has expanded her lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) in her state’s competitive Senate contest. The latest batch of votes to be counted reported Peltola leading by 2,517 first-choice votes which extended her lead of 637 from last week. She holds 48.63 percent of the vote, while Sullivan has 47.47…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) has expanded her lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) in her state’s competitive Senate contest.

The latest batch of votes to be counted reported Peltola leading by 2,517 first-choice votes which extended her lead of 637 from last week. She holds 48.63 percent of the vote, while Sullivan has 47.47 percent and Republican candidate Gerald Heikes received 2.23 percent of the vote, according to The Hill’s partner, Decision Desk HQ . Dan J. Sullivan Jr. has notched about 1.7 percent of the vote.

Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting, a candidate will still need to garner 50 percent of first-choice votes. If no candidate has greater than 50 percent of the vote after all first-choice ballots are counted, the state will run an instant runoff.

The tabulation eliminates the last-place candidate and redistributes their voters’ second, third and fourth-choice preferences. The process repeats until a candidate has a majority.

Before the latest batch of votes, an Alaskan Beacon analysis found Sullivan was favored to win in a runoff election. Now, Peltola’s lead puts her ahead of Sullivan even if the runoff was triggered.

The race drew national attention when a third-party spoiler candidate, who shared the same name as the incumbent Republican senator, advanced to the general election. Dan J. Sullivan Jr. has notched about 1.7 percent of the vote, per DDHQ.

Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s presence on the November ballot angered the Justice Department, which sued to block the certification of the election if the senator lost. The department argued that the spoiler candidate’s appearance on the ballots could confuse Alaskan voters but the case was dismissed by a federal judge.

The Beacon’s analysis conducted after Election Day also concluded that the results of the ranked-choice election indicated there was little to no voter confusion between the senator and the spoiler candidate.

A New York Times report alleged Peltola and national Democrats participated in an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. though she, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Daniel J. Sullivan have all denied any involvement in the reported effort to recruit spoiler candidates for the race.

Another court battle is ongoing as Peltola and Sullivan’s campaigns argue over whether the Democrat’s campaign can obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections.

President Trump has repeatedly weighed in on the race and on Tuesday morning wrote in a post on Truth Social , “Dan Sullivan PLUS Dan Sullivan wins the Alaska Election by thousands of votes. All votes going to the Fake Dan Sullivan, which was done solely for the purpose of fraud and confusion, should immediately be given to the Real Dan Sullivan (Senator!) -”

“Likewise the votes of the second fraudulent candidate, also put up by the Dems. There should be no question concerning this Rigged Election. Time is of the essence!!!” the president added.

Alaska’s vote count is expected to continue for several more days as state election officials transport ballots across the state’s remote parts. Ballots can arrive up to 15 days after the election so long as they are postmarked by Election Day.

articles.title: Trump signals surprising approach to choosing his successor as GOP's 2028 field grows
articles.summary: Trump says he may not endorse in the 2028 Republican Party presidential primary
articles.body: President Donald Trump says he may not put his thumb on the scale when it comes to picking the Republican Party's 2028 presidential nominee. "Probably, not necessarily," Trump said in a post-midterm election interview on CBS' "60 Minutes" when asked whether he will endorse in the primary to pick the next Republican nominee. "So I may or may not get involved... Maybe I'm better off not getting involved." Trump for months has touted the GOP's "great bench" when asked about the likely Republican field of contenders aiming to succeed him in the White House. The president reiterated that opinion after the GOP's drubbing in last week's midterm elections, as the party lost control of both the House and the Senate. VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS "I think we have an unbelievable bench of talent," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum in an election night interview on Fox News.. "We have a great group of talented people that I think would do a very good job." Early jockeying by the potential contenders began the morning after Election Day, with midterm post-mortems by Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis grabbing plenty of headlines. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "There's going to be a robust field of candidates that test the waters in Iowa, New Hampshire and South Carolina and that's exactly as it should be," Nicole Schlinger, a veteran Iowa-based Republican strategist, told Fox News Digital. "We're going to get an opportunity to see which approach to our message of where we as the Republican Party goes next is going to resonate the most with the grassroots voters who are going to show up and kick tires." Here's a look at the list of potential GOP presidential contenders in the burgeoning race to become the party's next standard-bearer and impact which direction the party will head in a post-Trump era. Vice President JD Vance The vice president has long been viewed as the likely frontrunner for the 2028 GOP nomination and Trump's heir apparent. But the conventional wisdom from pundits is that the shellacking the GOP took in the midterms has transformed what may have been a Vance coronation into a more competitive and crowded nomination battle. Vance kicked off the post-midterms debate last Wednesday morning with a roughly 600-word postmortem on X, blaming the war with Iran for the ballot box setbacks, in what some pundits viewed as an early pitch to eventually claim the MAGA and America First mantle. Even with last week's setbacks, Vance leads many of the early 2028 GOP presidential primary polls, has built a formidable fundraising network thanks in part to his role as the Republican National Committee's finance chair, and has a team of advisors and aides that would form the beginnings of a presidential campaign. Secretary of State Marco Rubio Rubio, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2016 GOP presidential nomination, is doing his best to stay far away from the 2028 spotlight. The former senator from Florida has long been floated by Trump and by pundits as a possible White House contender, and his support in early 2028 polls has soared. But Rubio has downplayed such speculation, and dismissed reports he was considering stepping down as secretary of state to lay the groundwork for a presidential run. Rubio, who has said a handful of times over the past year that he'd back Vance if the vice president decides to launch a White House campaign, was asked about 2028 Monday while taking questions from reporters during a stop in France. "I don't know why you're wasting your time," Rubio said. "I'm not going to talk about 2028 any longer. I'm just not going to talk about 2028 anymore." Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas The conservative firebrand senator from Texas, who was runner-up to Trump in the bruising 2016 presidential primaries, has made no secret that he may run for the White House again in 2028. In his post-Election Day assessment, Cruz described the midterms as a "blue tsunami" and warned that his party had lost touch with voters, particularly in the Lone Star State. "2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a-- kicking," Cruz wrote. "It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation." In a possible preview of the Republican primaries, Cruz has put plenty of daylight between himself and Vance over support for Israel, with Cruz spotlighting his support for the Israeli government. Boosting Cruz if he decides to run would be his top-ranked podcast, "Verdict with Ted Cruz," which has allowed the senator to build a massive grassroots network. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis The term-limited conservative Florida governor, who finishes up in Tallahassee at the start of the new year, ran for the White House in 2024. He was an early frontrunner before being decisively defeated by Trump. DeSantis held a news conference the morning after Election Day when he called the midterm election results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans across the country." "Let’s just be clear, that is going to hurt — not just for the next two years... That is something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he said. "We knew it could be worse. I don't think most of us thought it would be this bad." But DeSantis, who sat for a slew of media interviews in the wake of the midterms, repeatedly highlighted that "the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida." While 2028 buzz about DeSantis surged since last week's election, the governor took to social media on Friday to blast a report that he was planning a 2028 run, emphasizing, "I have not reached out to anybody about running for anything. Just another pathetic attempt to garner clicks." Former Vice President Mike Pence Pence, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, has said he has "no plans" to run for the White House again in 2028. But Pence has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year. And Trump's first vice president told Fox News Digital earlier this year that his fight to keep the Republican Party from drifting too far from its conservative roots and principles, amid a rise of populism in the GOP and big government creep during Trump's second administration, is "the calling of my life right now." Last week Pence argued, "The American people have rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism, and our majorities in Congress and state legislatures and governorships across the country paid the price." But he emphasized, "The conservative comeback starts today." Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp The conservative term-limited governor, who finishes out his tenure in Atlanta in two months, is also seen as a potential White House contender. In the wake of the midterm shellacking, Kemp spelled out a GOP vision centered on the "conservative principles of our party." "It’s time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come," the governor wrote. Former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin Youngkin, who instantly soared to political stardom after his 2021 gubernatorial victory energized Republicans a year after Trump lost the White House and the Senate in the 2020 election, has consistently downplayed talk of a 2028 presidential campaign. Instead, Youngkin has focused on his signature issue — education — by pushing to promote school choice programs through his recently formed national policy group Empowering America's Parents. Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie Christie, who unsuccessfully ran for the 2016 and 2024 GOP nominations, is seriously mulling a third run for the White House. "The midterms were a repudiation of the GOP and Donald Trump. It is time Republicans do the autopsy, learn the lessons and move forward," Christie, a vocal Republican critic of the president, argued in the days after last week's election. "The Trump era is over. He has led us to the greatest losses this country has seen for a party since Richard Nixon." Christie has said he'll decide on a presidential run in the next few months, telling Fox News Digital recently, "I think there’s a lot of flexibility on the timing." Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska Bacon, a former Air Force brigadier general who has at times split with Trump on foreign policy and national security issues, decided against running for re-election this year and exits Congress in two months. Bacon has said he is open to a potential run for president in 2028 or serving in a supporting role on another Republican candidate's ticket. Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders Sanders, the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee, earned national attention as Trump’s White House press secretary for much of his first term. Sanders, who made history four years ago as the first woman elected Arkansas governor and last week won re-election by double digits, is increasingly seen as a potential presidential contender. Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas Cotton, who took a hard look at a 2024 GOP presidential run before deciding against launching a campaign, was just re-elected. The senator, an Army veteran who served in combat in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars before becoming a rising star in the Republican Party and who was on Trump's running mate short list two years ago, is also viewed as a potential White House hopeful. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida Scott, a self-made multimillionaire and former two-term governor who's the wealthiest member of the Senate, also mulled a 2024 bid before running for re-election. Midterm election campaign trail stops in Iowa and New Hampshire — the two states that lead off the Republican presidential nominating calendar — sparked speculation that Scott was considering a 2028 campaign. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana Kennedy, who's up for re-election in 2028, has said he would consider a White House run instead of seeking another term in the Senate if he felt he could no longer be effective in the Senate or if he felt dissatisfied with the Republican presidential primary field. Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo Pompeo, a former four-term congressman from Kansas who served as CIA director and later as the top U.S. diplomat in Trump's first administration, also took a hard look at a 2024 run before passing. Asked last year about a 2028 bid, Pompeo told Fox News Digital, "We'll see what the good Lord brings in a couple of years." He's currently viewed by pundits as a possible contender. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky The vocal Republican critic of the president who relentlessly pressed for the release of the Epstein files before losing his bid for renomination earlier this year to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein has said he's "not ruling anything in or out" when it comes to a presidential bid. articles.title: Will Republicans finally stand up to Trump?
articles.summary: Republicans must break their blind loyalty to President Trump by challenging his policies on economics, foreign affairs, and ethics if they hope to avoid another electoral defeat in 2028.
articles.body:
If Republicans hope to survive the 2028 election, they will need to abandon their blind loyalty to President Trump — immediately, publicly and aggressively. Otherwise, many more of them will join the large ranks of just-defeated Republicans who got the electoral boot precisely because most of them were Trump loyalists.

Abondoning their “blind loyalty” doesn’t mean opposing Trump on everything. It just means standing up to him when he’s wrong on economic and foreign policy, which most Republicans have failed to do for the last two years.

Even now, there is jockeying to replace outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.). Some of those seeking the job are asserting they will take on the Democrats. The Wall Street Journal quotes Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as claiming, “I am battle-tested on the oversight front, and I know the Democrats’ playbook.” But what about being “battle-tested” against Trump?

Very few Republicans have been willing to publicly criticize the president’s policies and harsh personal attacks. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) occasionally pushed back, claiming he didn’t have the votes when Trump demanded he end the Senate filibuster and pass the Save America Act. That got Thune a round of boos from the MAGA crowd at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

Trump won’t make the next two years easy for Republicans. When other presidents suffered a midterm rout — for example, President Bill Clinton in 1994 and President Geroge W. Bush in 2006 — they often acknowledged the loss and made some course corrections. Not Trump.

By replacing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with hardliner Stephen Miller — you could call him “Trump’s id” — the president is telegraphing that he plans to double down on his worst instincts and policies. That’s going to create a real challenge for Republicans who know they need to separate themselves from the president and his policies but fear his and MAGA’s backlash.

Take tariffs, for example. The voters hate Trump’s arbitrary, cost-increasing tariffs , which is an important reason why they voted against Republicans. Democrats have pledged to introduce legislation to repeal or restrict Trump’s tariffs , perhaps starting with Canada.

Democrats will claim the president has grossly abused his limited tariff authority, that repealing tariffs would be one of the fastest ways to lower prices and improve relations with our allies, and the Constitution vests the power to tax — and a tariff is a tax — in Congress. Correct on all points. Then Democrats will dare Republicans to vote against the legislation.

Trump — the self-proclaimed “ tariff man ” — will almost surely oppose the effort and demand Republicans vote no, forcing Republicans in Congress to choose.

Of course, Trump would likely veto any anti-tariff legislation. Would Republicans join Democrats in overriding that veto?

Or take the war with Iran. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) says Democrats will vote to defund the war with Iran, though not general defense spending. They will claim that ending the war will help bring gas prices down, that the war has become a quagmire, and that Trump should have sought input from our allies, the public and especially Congress, since the Constitution vests Congress with the power to declare and fund a war. Again, all true.

Democrats will dare Republicans to vote against their effort, even though Trump will oppose it.

In addition, Democrats may try to move legislation that restricts Trump’s personal vanity projects, like his proposed Trump arch and renaming the Kennedy Center after himself — distractions that have greatly irritated voters . Will Republicans join Democrats to stop the president?

Finally, voters said corruption was one of their top issues. Democrats will open investigations into several areas of the Trump family businesses, especially his sons. Republicans were very eager to pursue Hunter Biden ’s shady financial dealings and efforts to profit off his father’s position. Will Republicans be at least open to investigating the president’s sons and take appropriate steps if they discover corruption?

When the whole world could see that President Joe Biden’s mental and physical capacities were declining, Democrats denied it and publicly and aggressively defended the president. That cost them dearly in the 2024 election.

Could something similar happen to Republicans in 2028 if they refuse to take on Trump?

The irony is that in rejecting some of Trump’s priorities, Republicans could reaffirm their long-held principles that made them the conservative party: free trade, fiscal responsibility, free markets, limited government, and, perhaps most importantly, the constitutional separation of powers.

The 2028 presidential campaign is underway, and Democratic presidential candidates would love to spend the next two years reminding voters they can’t lower prices and root out corruption because Republicans would rather side with Trump. Ronald Reagan’s most famous speech, in 1964, was “ A Time for Choosing .” It’s time for Republicans to choose.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.

articles.title: Mike Johnson blasts Massie’s ‘shameful’ push to oust Hegseth
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Tuesday criticized Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The House is set to hold a procedural vote Tuesday evening on the eight articles of impeachment the Kentucky lawmaker introduced the previous day. Johnson called the effort to oust Hegseth “shameful” and accused Massie of…
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Tuesday criticized Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The House is set to hold a procedural vote Tuesday evening on the eight articles of impeachment the Kentucky lawmaker introduced the previous day.

Johnson called the effort to oust Hegseth “shameful” and accused Massie of using this measure as a “political gambit for attention,” in comments to reporters on Capitol Hill.

“I expect that we’re going to defeat that, one way or the other, and we’ll get on with the business,” Johnson told reporters.

“The idea that you would impeach the secretary of War at a time of international conflict sends a terrible message to our enemies and our allies, and we are not going to play that game,” he continued, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense. “You don’t impeach a Cabinet secretary lightly.”

Additionally, the Speaker commended Hegseth for his response to the impeachment effort in a Tuesday morning press conference, saying the Defense secretary did an “extraordinary job.”

In a 30-minute briefing at the Pentagon, Hegseth cast Massie as a “single rogue legislator” who was motivated by “personal animus for the president.”

“It puts a target on the backs of American warriors, by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time,” Hegseth said. “This is not patriotism; this is sabotage.”

Massie accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution and federal laws with the U.S. military operations in Iran and elsewhere.

It is unclear whether the measure will garner enough Republican support to pass the House. Massie told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in a Monday evening interview he was hoping to gain support from retiring GOP lawmakers and those who just barely secured their reelection last week.

President Trump has stood by his Defense secretary, rating his press conference performance on Tuesday morning an “‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS” in a Truth Social post . Trump also ripped Massie as a “disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman.”

articles.title: Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t back Schumer in Senate leadership vote
articles.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) declined to back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as he prepares to seek his caucus’s support to become majority leader beginning in January. Asked by reporters outside the Capitol if she would back her home state’s senator for the top spot in the upper chamber given calls for new leadership…
articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) declined to back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as he prepares to seek his caucus’s support to become majority leader beginning in January.

Asked by reporters outside the Capitol if she would back her home state’s senator for the top spot in the upper chamber given calls for new leadership in the party, Ocasio-Cortez said that would be up to members of the Senate.

“I think that this is a sentiment that is seen in a lot of places,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “So how the Senate navigates that, that’s up to their decision.”

Schumer, who will turn 76 later this month, has faced skepticism and calls to step down from some younger members of his party. Multiple incoming Senate Democrats — Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine) — have said they will not back Schumer for majority leader.

Still, the leader said he had secured enough support to become Senate leader, something he needs a majority of his caucus to do. After Democrats’ massive victories in the midterms, the party’s now-sizable majority in the upper chamber allows him to win a vote even if some Senate Democrats do not back him.

If Schumer runs for reelection in 2028, he would be 84 at the end of his next term. Ocasio-Cortez is seen as a potential challenger to Schumer in the Democratic primary but pivoted when asked if she would take him on, saying Americans do not want to hear about another election.

“The last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “They want to know about the investigations we’re going to be starting, what is the legislation that we’re going to be starting … what we’re going to do with the power that they just gave us.”

If she does not challenge Schumer, the progressive Democrat is also seen as a possible presidential candidate in 2028. A political action committee run by progressive activists, called “Ready for AOC,” recently launched in an attempt to draw her into the race.

Ocasio-Cortez has been candid that she is considering her options — presidential campaign or primary challenge.

“I think that anything is possible at this juncture,” Ocasio-Cortez told ABC News’ “This Week” in August.

articles.title: Inclusion was the big winner in the midterms
articles.summary: Americans celebrated diversity by delivering a long list of electoral firsts.
articles.body:
The postmortem on the blue wave began even before states had finished counting the votes. Gleeful Democrats foresee an “ end to the Trump era ,” while Republicans have begun a rancorous debate over whether their own president lost them the House and the Senate.

In addition to the Democrats, the big winner was inclusion. Americans celebrated diversity by delivering a long list of electoral firsts.

Texas chose its first Hispanic woman governor . New Mexicans elected the first Native American woman governor in the history of the country. Minnesota is sending the first Native American woman to the Senate and New Hampshire elected the first openly gay man to the upper house. Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first African-American woman governor in U.S. history, elected in Georgia, once a bastion of the Jim Crow South .

Perhaps the biggest testament to the triumph of tolerance over bigotry came in Michigan. In one of the most bitterly contested Senate races in history during which Republicans spent millions on vicious attack ads and the president called him a jihadist , Abdul El-Sayed (D) defeated Mike Rogers by approximately 7 percentage points .

Even in down-ballot races, candidates broke barriers. Nabeela Syed flipped a Republican seat to become the first Muslim woman elected to the Illinois Senate.

Pundits will be quick to point out that these victories had more to do with hating Trump than loving Democrats. Be that as it may, the voters rejected identity politics and focused on issues. Republicans had based their gerrymandering plans on race and ethnicity, seeking to dilute the African American vote and strengthen the Hispanic.

The plan backfired, especially in Texas , where Republicans lost 4 of 5 seats the new map was supposed to help them win. Across the country, Democrats made significant gains with every demographic . The war on woke no longer garners votes.

However, impressive as this progress is, much more needs to be done. Women and minorities are still underrepresented in Congress, state houses and governor’s mansions. Voters elected a record number of women governors , but that will bring the total to just 17 of 50.

The Democrats got their blue wave, but figuring out what the election reveals about the future of the party and who should be its 2028 standard bearer will be challenging. When it comes to electability, the picture painted by the midterms is murky.

Those on the left will point to El-Sayed’s victory, the reelection of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Minn.) and the election of Nithya Raman as mayor of Los Angeles as evidence that progressives and even socialists are electable. They also see the high turnout among young voters demanding change as a good omen. Establishment Democrats will counter that overtly Christian candidates won the races for U.S. Senate in Kansas and Texas .

Both are right. The midterms reveal that no national formula for electability works. The elections confirmed the old adage that all politics are local. Rev. Adam Hamilton (D), for example , won his Kansas Senate race on a campaign of affordability that appealed to farmers facing high diesel and fertilizer costs and suburbanites struggling to pay for gas and food.

Voters on both sides of the aisle agree on one thing: They are tired of politics as usual. In three of the U.S. Senate seats the Democrats flipped, the candidates had never held elected office: El-Sayed in Michigan, Hamilton in Kansas and Annie Andrews in South Carolina .

Younger voters in particular are tired of what they see as geriatric leadership. The midterms may usher in a generational change in the leadership of both parties. In the current Congress , members average two decades older than the general public; three out of four senators are baby boomers or from the silent generation and most Americans want age and term limits.

So, while the Democrats have much to celebrate, they also have cause for concern. Their party remains deeply unpopular with an average favorability rating of just 39 percent according to recent polling, only slightly better than the Republican rating of 38 percent Those numbers indicate that far from being an endorsement of the party, the midterms represent a demand that whoever governs make life better for ordinary Americans.

Partisan politics notwithstanding, however, the diversity of last week’s winners is something to celebrate.

Tom Mockaitis is a professor of history at DePaul University and the author of “ Violent Extremists: Understanding the Domestic and International Terrorist Threat .”

articles.title: Trump gives Hegseth an A+
articles.summary: President Trump gives Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth an “A” plus for his work at the Pentagon following outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introducing eight articles of impeachment against him. “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER,” Trump wrote on…
articles.body:
President Trump gives Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth an “A” plus for his work at the Pentagon following outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introducing eight articles of impeachment against him.

“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Tuesday.

In another post , Trump linked to Hegseth’s Tuesday Pentagon briefing , saying it was a “great job by Pete Hegseth — A MUST SEE.”

While Trump has publicly backed Hegseth in private, the commander-in-chief has asked advisers and allies about the defense secretary’s standing, The Hill previously reported . One of those sources described the defense chief as being in “a lot of trouble,” while the other said it wasn’t clear how much his position was in jeopardy.

Hegseth called Massie’s impeachment effort a “farce” and “stunt” at his first press briefing in 189 days.

“In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of War or secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that,” he continued.

The defense secretary further accused Massie of attempting to impeach him over policy disagreements, calling it a “personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”

“That’s what it is. Policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause,” he added.

The impeachment articles accused the defense secretary of violating the Constitution and other laws during U.S. military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) signaled his support for the move, while GOP lawmakers across the aisle remain divided on their support.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Kansas), chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told reporters he thought Hegseth “made a very, very good presentation,” adding that he was “unclear why this is being taken up so quickly in the House,” per the Washington Sun’s Joe Gould.

When asked if he believed Hegseth had the votes, Wicker responded: “I would hope so.”

articles.title: Senate Republicans suspend leadership election amid demands for ‘a plan’ from John Thune
articles.summary: Senate Republicans on Tuesday paused their meeting to elect leaders after Senate conservatives demanded “a plan” for the lame-duck session and the next Congress when Democrats will be in the majority. Republican senators streamed out of the Old Senate Chamber after huddling in the historic room for nearly two hours to discuss their future after…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans on Tuesday paused their meeting to elect leaders after Senate conservatives demanded “a plan” for the lame-duck session and the next Congress when Democrats will be in the majority.

Republican senators streamed out of the Old Senate Chamber after huddling in the historic room for nearly two hours to discuss their future after losing at least seven seats in last week’s election.

“We’re still discussing. We ran out of time,” Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) told reporters after senators broke up the meeting.

Johnson said Republican senators would reconvene at 2 p.m. to resume their discussion about the future leadership of the conference.

Thune and other members of his team are pressing for GOP colleagues to vote today on re-electing him as Senate Republican leader but they want to give members of the conference all the time they need to voice their views.

Senate Steering Committee Chairman Rick Scott (R-Fla.) said he and several other Republican colleagues are demanding a clear roadmap from Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) about how he will handle the rest of the lame-duck session and the incoming Senate and House Democratic majorities in 2027 and beyond.

He said that it’s yet to be decided whether the leadership vote will take place Tuesday afternoon.

“We haven’t decided whether it’s going to be delayed. We had a conversation and more people wanted to speak,” he said.

Scott spoke during the private session and urged his colleagues to adopt a plan before electing a new leadership team, citing his years of executive leadership in the business world.

“I said I’m a business guy. … I started a lot of businesses, I built a lot of businesses, I turned around a lot of businesses. The first thing is you have a plan of what you want to accomplish then you put together a management team,” he said.

“I want to hear a plan. I’ve been up here eight years, I’ve never heard a plan in a year,” he said. “We have 55 days until the Democrats take over. I said so I want to know what we’re going to do between now and then to get stuff done.”

A third Republican senator who requested anonymity described the morning meeting as a “lively discussion” and said Republican colleagues want to hear “a plan” from Thune for the lame-duck session before voting to re-elect him as leader.

articles.title: Alsobrooks, Tillis to introduce veteran home loan program bill in Senate
articles.summary: A bipartisan Senate duo will introduce legislation to help support veterans who utilize Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) home loan programs, according to the bill’s text exclusively obtained by The Hill. Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) plan to introduce the VA Home Loan Navigator Act as soon as today — establishing a…
articles.body:
A bipartisan Senate duo will introduce legislation to help support veterans who utilize Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) home loan programs, according to the bill’s text exclusively obtained by The Hill.

Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) plan to introduce the VA Home Loan Navigator Act as soon as today — establishing a program to support borrowers through financial counseling and other services meant to help veterans through the loan process. Hundreds of thousands VA-backed home loans are granted each year with many veterans relying on VA support to afford housing.

“Our veterans have earned the opportunity to achieve the American dream of owning a home and we have a responsibility to ensure they have the resources and support they need to make it happen,” Tillis said in a statement to The Hill.

The VA home loan program — started in 1944 in an effort to aid servicemembers as they returned from war — has been amended a number of times to expand access, raise loan amounts and help homeless veterans.

But in recent years as pandemic era assistance programs end, foreclosure rates have been on the rise, putting veterans at risk.

The Alsobrooks-Tillis bill instructs the VA Secretary to partner with nonprofit organizations, who will be trained on the loan process and provide assistance to borrowers. The certified service providers will be able to provide individualized counseling for loss mitigation and foreclosure prevention, coordinate between borrowers, mortgage servicers and the VA and assist with VA loan eligibility issues.

Services are voluntary and at no cost to borrowers.

“The VA Home Loan Navigator Act will provide veterans with free, trusted guidance to help navigate the homebuying and mortgage process, understand their benefits, and address challenges that could put their homes at risk,” Tillis said.

Rep. Veronica Escobar (D-Texas) and Rep. Jack Bergman (R- Mich.) introduced a similar bill of the same name earlier this year. The House bill is not identical to the new Alsobrooks-Tillis bill, but both have the goal of providing support by partnering with outside organizations.

At least six other bills have been introduced during the 119th Congress that address VA home loans. The VA Home Loan Program Reform Act , which became law in July, works to avoid foreclosure on primary residences through a limited payment assistance program.

Alsobrooks told The Hill in a statement that Congress is obligated to do more to thank and provide for those who served the country. She said veterans deserve access to affordable health care, groceries, gas and housing.

“I am so proud to partner with my colleague Senator Tillis to introduce this critical legislation that will support veterans through the mortgage and loan process and make the American dream of owning a home a reality for those who have served our country,” Alsobrooks said.

articles.title: Cornyn meets with Sen-elect Talarico, describes him as 'basically ... a good person'

articles.body: Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, has said that he met with Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico in Washington, D.C., on Monday after previously meeting with him on Friday in Texas. articles.title: Bacon plans to vote ‘no’ on Hegseth impeachment
articles.summary: Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) said he plans to vote against adopting articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ahead of the Tuesday afternoon vote in the House. The Nebraska Republican, who did not seek reelection in 2026, said he has his own problems with Hegseth that are not named in the impeachment articles. “I…
articles.body:
Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) said he plans to vote against adopting articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ahead of the Tuesday afternoon vote in the House.

The Nebraska Republican, who did not seek reelection in 2026, said he has his own problems with Hegseth that are not named in the impeachment articles.

“I don’t really align with the impeachment itself,” Bacon told reporters Tuesday. “If we talk about firing 80 generals and not spending appropriated money, I’d feel a little differently about it.”

“I have separate complaints about the secretary that’s not in the impeachment,” Hegseth said.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) announced articles of impeachment against Hegseth Monday, arguing that he violated the Constitution by fighting the war in Iran without congressional authorization. Other articles accuse him of breaking the law through U.S. military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) for telling servicemembers not to follow illegal orders.

Hegseth responded in a news conference at the Pentagon Tuesday morning, calling Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” and saying the impeachment is “a political spectacle.” Massie lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year.

But with Republicans controlling the House until January, Tuesday’s impeachment vote needs at least a few Republicans to vote with Democrats for the resolution to succeed.

As a retiring member who is sometimes critical of the Trump administration, Bacon is a key vote that could be decisive. Another retiring Republican, Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), said Tuesday that she would not vote to impeach either, even as she has been very critical of the Iran war.

“I will not be voting to impeach,” Mace wrote on the social platform X. “The Iran war is through no fault of his own and he should not be the one scapegoated for it. I fully support the changes Hegseth has made to the [Defense Department] to make our fighting force the very best it can be.”

Bacon said one reason he is not voting to impeach is because he wants the U.S. “to win in Iran.”

“I want us to win in Iran,” Bacon said. “Iran’s been killing us for 47 years. I have a different perspective than Massie on this.”

Even if the vote fails, Democrats could easily impeach Hegseth when their sizable majority is sworn in Jan. 3. If Hegseth is impeached in the House, two-thirds of senators are needed to convict and remove him from office.

articles.title: Mamdani makes behind-the-scenes moves to shape 2028 Democratic presidential race
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is meeting with labor leaders to rally progressives around a 2028 presidential candidate if AOC stays out.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is quietly working towards a new goal: to become a progressive kingmaker in the burgeoning battle for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. The socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, who can't run for president himself because he's not a natural-born U.S. citizen, has been meeting behind closed doors with labor leaders to highlight the need for a union-aligned or left-wing candidate to seek the presidency. The mayor's moves come as he's reportedly said he's uncertain whether progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, his close political ally, will run for the White House. According to Axios, which was first to report the news, Mamdani is concerned that if Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it could leave progressives without a standard-bearer to face off against a more centrist presidential frontrunner in the primary battle. WILL TRUMP SIT OUT MAKING A 2028 ENDORSEMENT IN THE RACE TO SUCCEED HIM? Mamdani, who is seen as a major powerbroker for the left wing of the Democratic Party after his historic 2025 mayoral election victory, argues that the progressive movement can't waste its momentum coming out of last week's trouncing of Republicans in the midterm elections, as Democrats won a massive House majority and control of the Senate. A source familiar with Mamdani's 2028 conversations told Axios the mayor "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise," Meanwhile, Ocasio-Cortez is publicly pumping the brakes on speculation she'll launch a presidential campaign or bid for the Senate in New York, even as a newly formed group of activists is urging her run for the White House. VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS "I think the thing that's important here is the last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election. And what they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters Monday night, pointing to the midterms. The comments from Ocasio-Cortez, who was re-elected last week to a fifth term representing parts of New York City, came hours after the formal launch of Ready for AOC, a political group working to encourage her to run for president by showing her she has legions of supporters ready to mobilize on her behalf. "A people-powered movement asking Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for President in 2028. No campaign. No money. Just names," is how the group described itself on social media. But Ocasio-Cortez said voters are more concerned about congressional Democrats' immediate legislative agenda rather than speculating about the next election. "I think people are less concerned about the horse race, and they want to know: What are the investigations we're going to be starting? What is the legislation that we're going to be starting?" she said. Veteran Democratic strategist David Plouffe, campaign manager for former President Barack Obama's landmark 2008 White House victory and a senior advisor on then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 bid, said last week, "If AOC runs, she's going to start, 20-25%, probably. The question is, can she add to that? If she doesn't run, then that is wide open. That's where I think someone like Abdul may say, 'Even though I just won, should I look at it?'" SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Plouffe, who was speaking at a forum hosted by Harvard University's Institute of Politics, was referring to Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who made history last week as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. "That's the thing about this race. It's so wide open that there may be some people run who surprise us. I also think there'll be some people who don't run who'll surprise us," Plouffe added. Ocasio-Cortez said in September that she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a White House run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker. "I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a fundraising email to supporters. The now-37-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a New York Times interview two months ago that her decision, which could happen sometime after the midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?" Schumer, who turns 76 later this month, has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for sixth six-year term in the Senate. Allies of the soon-to-be six-term congressman last week launched a draft committee called "Run Ro" to build support and raise funds for a potential 2028 presidential campaign.

articles.title: Joe Biden too sick to narrate book, do events, forgot Bob Dole died?
articles.summary: I can’t help but point this out again: Right now we are halfway through Donald Trump’s second term, a term that Biden had sought to serve. Had his team successfully covered up his failing health situation, and had he won the election, he would be president right now.
articles.body:
Former President Biden is releasing a new book called “Promise Me, America.” It’s his post-presidential memoir, and I’m sure everyone is looking to hear about his decision to quit the 2024 presidential race in his own words. But notably, we will not be hearing this in his own voice. Biden was unable to narrate the audio version of the book, and he’s going to be doing far fewer events than he had planned, according to an announcement he made on social media.

“While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families. My doctors continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment. And the prayers and kind words and well wishes from so many of you have meant more to me and Jill and our family than you can ever know.”

“Some days are better than others,” he continues. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves.”

I wish Biden well, and so should all Americans. I hope he makes a full recovery. Cancer is a terrible illness, and like most people, I know loved ones who have succumbed to it.

But I can’t help but point this out again: Right now we are halfway through Donald Trump’s second term, a term that Biden had sought to serve. Had his team successfully covered up his failing health situation, and had he won the election, he would be president right now. In reality, of course, it’s impossible to imagine him actually serving as president in such a state, and so Kamala Harris would have taken over by now.

Biden’s team maintains that he did not find out about the cancer until well after the election. Maybe that’s true. But everybody who saw Biden up close in the final year of his presidency should have known that this man was too old to be president, let alone for another four years — that age had caught up with him, and was impacting his mental faculties and his communicative abilities. He had stopped meeting with his Cabinet, wandered off during events, needed tape on the ground to serve as arrows directing him around donor meetings.

And now, according to new details from Alex Thompson and Kate Tapper in their book, “Original Sin,” in 2024, Biden appeared to forget that his old Senate colleague Bob Dole had died several years before. He also seemed to think his son Beau was still alive, fighting his own cancer diagnosis.

On X, Biden boosters complain that Thompson and Tapper were still pursuing the truth about Biden’s infirmity, prompting Josh Barro to quip: “Biden is ‘allowed’ to do whatever he wants. It’s just notable that Biden wanted to be the Democratic nominee again when he lacks the capacity even to narrate his own audiobook.”

Yeah, that’s the problem. We are now living through the hypothetical Biden second term, and we are seeing just how badly off he is. I think that’s sad for him, but it underscores just how reprehensibly his whole team acted in concealing him from us — from the American people — in order protect the lie that he could serve for another four years. And we can’t forget it.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Family unsure where 8-year-old Haitian boy is being held after ICE detention
articles.summary: An 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken by federal immigration officers during a routine immigration appointment in California last week, prompting lawmakers to question the boy’s whereabouts. The boy, who is a third grader at Fay Elementary School in San Diego, Calif., lost his Temporary Protected Status after the Supreme Court ended legal protections for Haitians in…
articles.body:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken by federal immigration officers during a routine immigration appointment in California last week, prompting lawmakers to question the boy’s whereabouts.

The boy, who is a third grader at Fay Elementary School in San Diego, Calif., lost his Temporary Protected Status after the Supreme Court ended legal protections for Haitians in June , according to a report by NBC News citing a letter from school district officials. He was called to meet with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer last week and was taken to the appointment by his uncle who has been taking care of him since his father was deported last year, the report said.

Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said, “the child was taken into custody and subsequently transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement,” NBC reported.

California Sens. Alex Padilla (D) and Adam B. Schiff (D) along with four other lawmakers sent a letter to federal officials on Tuesday, expressing concerns about the wellbeing of the boy and requesting confirmation on his whereabouts.

“We express concerns about the basis for this action and the harm it may cause a young child who appeared for his required hearing before the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR),” the letter read.

“We also request confirmation on the child’s whereabouts, whether his family is aware of his location, and what steps your agencies are taking to ensure he can be reunited with them,” it added.

A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security told NBC that ICE officers said they could not confirm if the man who accompanied the boy to the appointment was related to him and “the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor.”

“Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household,” the spokesperson said in the NBC report.

The events surrounding the Haitian boy is among several other instances marking the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration. Recently, a 21-year-old Wisconsin state trooper of South African origin, was detained by ICE and released a day later.

Immigration has been a key focus for the second Trump administration. Democrats across the country have campaigned against the crackdown with some even calling to abolish ICE.
