articles.title: How Republicans lost the Hispanic vote
articles.summary: There is no attainable conservative movement without the Hispanic electorate.
articles.body:
Last week, America sent more than a message to Capitol Hill — it delivered a resounding verdict.

Democrats will control both chambers of the 120th Congress, with a House majority exceeding 250 seats . A blue tidal wave swept through districts President Trump carried just two years ago. Republicans can blame turnout, candidates or maps, but for sensible Americans, the truth is much simpler: They lost on affordability, they lost on the war in Iran, and they lost on immigration.

The numbers are screaming at us. According to one exit poll, 63 percent of voters called military action against Iran the wrong decision, and nearly eight in 10 said inflation is causing hardship in their homes. Then there is the data that should keep every conservative strategist awake at night. In 2024, 46 percent of Hispanic voters supported Trump; on Election Night, Republican House candidates won just 35 percent . That is an 11-point collapse in 24 months.

Look at Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 1988 , defeating Ken Paxton decisively. In the Rio Grande Valley, where maps were redrawn to hand Republicans new seats, Hispanic families swung hard back toward Democrats . Even in Florida, the governor’s race came down to just a 1.3-point margin .

Here is what the consultants will not tell you: This was not a rejection of border security. The vast majority of commonsense Americans want every gang member, trafficker and violent criminal deported as quickly as possible. I want that. Our churches want that. What went wrong was something else entirely.

The grievous error was targeting the 65-year-old grandmother who has lived here for 20 years, who makes tortillas or cleans homes. She worships in our evangelical churches and our Catholic parishes. Her children were born and raised here. She has never had a parking ticket, does not depend on government entitlements, and works 40 to 60 hours a week. The Migration Policy Institute found that 61 percent of deportations of immigrants with more than 10 years in this country involved people with no criminal record. Raiding Home Depot parking lots and restaurant kitchens is not who we are as Americans. It’s certainly not the heart and soul of the conservative movement.

This is the fruit of the enforcement machine Kristi Noem built at the Department of Homeland Security, and of political myopia among those who neglected the Hispanic electorate. But let’s be clear-eyed about what happened: There is no attainable conservative movement without the Hispanic electorate.

Hispanic Americans are the firewall. We are the firewall against socialism and communism, against the mutilation of children, against men in women’s sports, against antisemitism, against lawlessness and anarchy.

But you cannot get into our hearts while you are invading our kitchens and harming our churches.

All that being said, there is reason for hope. Within hours of the results, the president said on Fox News that he can work with Democrats, including on immigration . That is wisdom. It is also an acknowledgment that the problem was never the conservative vision — it was the execution.

If Republicans and independent-minded Americans are truly reading the tea leaves this week, they will discover that building a lasting coalition requires elevating leaders who are fluent in both the language of our abuelas and the language of our Constitution. And a serious prescription for 2028 is an immigration philosophy that secures the border without breaking families.

The firewall stands ready. The question is whether the party is ready to honor it.

Rev. Samuel Rodriguez is lead pastor of New Season Church in Sacramento, Calif., and president of the National Hispanic Christian Leadership Conference. He has advised three U.S. presidents and is the first Latino to participate in multiple presidential inauguration ceremonies.

articles.title: Bill O’Reilly slams Mullin: ‘He’s worse than Noem’
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly blasted Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s leadership after big Republican losses in the midterms, saying he “couldn’t have been worse.” O’Reilly, a staunch conservative and usually a supporter of President Trump, said the administration went “too far” on the issue of immigration, blaming it for losses in Latino support around the…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly blasted Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s leadership after big Republican losses in the midterms, saying he “couldn’t have been worse.”

O’Reilly, a staunch conservative and usually a supporter of President Trump, said the administration went “too far” on the issue of immigration, blaming it for losses in Latino support around the country.

“When people are getting beat up in the streets by federal agents, you need to say why,” O’Reilly said.

In an interview on CBS News’s “60 Minutes” after the election, Trump said he did think immigration enforcement went too far in some cases and expressed openness to working with Democrats on immigration reform.

The former Fox News anchor blamed Mullin directly for how the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has carried out enforcement, arguing he is worse than former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, who Trump replaced earlier this year.

“This Markwayne Mullin guy couldn’t have been worse. He’s worse than Noem,” O’Reilly said. “Never explained, arrogant as hell. What are you doing?”

The “No Spin News” host suggested that if he were in charge, Mullin would not be in the job.

“If it were me, Mullin would be in the Bahamas right now taking in the sun,” O’Reilly said.

Other Republicans, including O’Reilly’s former Fox News colleague Sean Hannity, called for a change in immigration policy. Hannity said after the election that Trump should seek public input to determine his immigration policy going forward.

Despite the political blowback, Mullin said after the midterms that “deportations will continue.”

While it was a strength for him in the 2024 campaign, immigration slowly became a political liability for Trump throughout his second term.

Controversial tactics, mass deportations and multiple fatal shootings slowly dragged down the president’s approval on immigration, even as border security remains a strong suit. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted just before the midterms found that just 37 percent approved of Trump’s handling of immigration, while 55 percent disapproved.

It is one of a few issues that may have hurt GOP support with Latino voters in the midterm elections, a group that had been steadily shifting right in the past few cycles. Preliminary New York Times voter poll data shows that Democrats won Latino voters by 41 points nationally, a 30-point shift left from 2024.

And in Texas, a state with a large Latino population, the shift was even more pronounced. The Times found that Sen.-elect James Talarico (D) won Latino voters by 46 points in the Lone Star State, a 46-point shift left from 2024.

articles.title: Trump baselessly casts doubt on midterm election results
articles.summary: Donald Trump has learned nothing and continues to make a habit out of undermining our election process and throwing around baseless accusations.
articles.body:
It was only a matter of time before the election denial began.

For a brief moment, it seemed President Trump might actually accept a political defeat . Democrats just delivered a sweeping rebuke to Republicans, taking control of both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats, and making historic gains in statehouses across the country.

But it was too good to be true. On Monday, nearly a week after the election, Trump took to Truth Social and wrote : “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”

And there it is. The familiar suggestion that an election he didn’t like the outcome of must somehow be illegitimate.

Now, Trump is right about one thing: The polls were wrong. But not in the way he’s suggesting. They underestimated the Democrats.

In Georgia, Democrats outperformed final polling averages. In Texas, James Talarico’s Senate victory over Ken Paxton was about 9 points stronger than polling projected. South Carolina is particularly notable: Annie Andrews won a Republican-held Senate seat after final polling averages showed Republicans narrowly ahead.

Mississippi deserves attention, too. Scott Colom’s Senate bid is extremely competitive, and if he wins, it would mark a huge shift in the state, where conservatives have dominated for nearly 150 years.

In another post, the president seemed to take issue with Texas in particular. Greg Abbott is still in office and Republicans control the legislature, so how then were Democrats able to rig that state’s elections? Gina Hinojosa defeated a three-term governor and Republicans’ redistricting efforts failed to. Mystery solved. There is no evidence of fraud, and the president is likely not planning to offer any evidence either.

You may remember earlier this year, Trump sat down with Kristen Welker and insisted the 2020 election and the California primary elections were both rigged.

TRUMP : “The election was rigged, it was a dirty election. And it’s happening again right now in California.”

WELKER: “You’ve never presented evidence that the 2020 election was rigged. Where’s the evidence to that? Republicans are doing well in California.”

TRUMP: No they’re not, they’re dropping fast because it’s a rigged election. It takes four days, they’re cheating.”

WELKER : “Do you have evidence to support that?”

The exchange resulted in the president abruptly getting up and leaving the interview .

Donald Trump has learned nothing and continues to make a habit out of undermining our election process and throwing around baseless accusations. In 2016, even after winning, he falsely claimed millions of undocumented immigrants had voted illegally. In 2020, after losing to Joe Biden, he spent months claiming the election was stolen.

Remember what followed: pressure on Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, to find 11,780 votes , the fake elector scheme across seven states, and his demands that Mike Pence interfere with the electoral count.

Then came January 6 . The Capitol attack was not disconnected from those efforts. It happened as Congress was certifying Biden’s victory, after Trump had spent weeks telling supporters the election was stolen.

This is déjà vu in the worst way. Voters sent a message about the economy, the administration’s policies and the direction of the country. Yet instead of reflecting on why so many Americans rejected his party, Trump is once again casting doubt on the machinery.

We saw where that road led in 2020. Accept the results and make the necessary changes, or prepare for a repeat in 2028.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Hegseth says impeachment ‘not about me’:

We’ll fill you in, don’t worry. In today’s issue: House vote on Hegseth impeachment Senate GOP leadership vote delayed Peltola expands lead on Sullivan in Alaska Gas prices…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday. Did you sleep (or commute) your way through Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s 8 a.m. EST press conference? We’ll fill you in, don’t worry.

Peltola expands lead on Sullivan in Alaska

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Joshua Feldstein, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com and jfeldstein@thehill.com .

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held his first press briefing in 189 days on Tuesday morning, a day after Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief.

House lawmakers are expected to vote on Tuesday at 5:30 p.m. EST on whether they will remove the Defense secretary, who has been in the spotlight.

Massie’s impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of abusing his powers, including the Iran war, the killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters and the U.S.’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.

“Make no mistake about what is happening. This is not about me. Politicians in Washington have accused the sailors and the pilots who struck narco terrorist boats of war crimes for doing their job,” Hegseth said at Tuesday’s press conference.

“Senators in cute videos have suggested the same. This resolution is the next step. Put the secretary on trial today, and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow,” he continued.

Deflecting Vance’s remarks : Following Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections, Vice President Vance blamed the results on the Iran war. In response, Hegseth said he was “not going to exchange any finger pointing” with the vice president and that he “greatly” respected Vance.

“Thankfully, politics is not really my thing. I do the Department of War and making sure we’re prepared and ready. So a lot of people are going to look at the conflict and assess it,” Hegseth said on Tuesday morning.

So what if it’s unpopular! : “It was done for the right reasons to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said, defending the war with Iran.

“As [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio said, I think quite well, it’s not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary, and that’s certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking,” he continued.

President Trump took to Truth Social on Tuesday following the Pentagon chief’s press briefing, saying “Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”

Is an impeachment possible? : Until January, the GOP holds possession of the House and Senate.

But with Vance’s criticism of the Iran war being at the forefront of everyone’s minds following the party’s defeat in last week’s midterms, there could be attendance issues, and it’s not clear all Republicans will fall in line.

Several GOP lawmakers including Reps. French Hill (Ark.) and James Comer (Ky.) have voiced their concerns over the conflict in Iran and the administration’s handling of the situation.

“There’s a lot of questions about Hegseth,” Comer told NewsNation on Friday. “We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran.”

Key GOP no votes : Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb,), who has been critical over Hegseth and the Iran war, said he will most likely vote no on the impeachment because he says he doesn’t align with it.

“Mr. Massie, who’s anti-Iran, anti-Ukraine, anti-Israel. I mean, I don’t really align with the impeachment itself,” Bacon told reporters on Tuesday.

“I have separate complaints about the Secretary that’s not in the impeachment,” he continued.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told reporters that he is “unclear why this is being taken up so quickly in the House.”

“I thought he [Hegseth] made a very, very good presentation,” Wicker added.

Republicans in the House and Senate are set to hold leadership elections Tuesday after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories last week. But there are calls in both chambers to delay the process.

Surprise in the Senate: In a last-minute push on Tuesday, GOP senators decided to suspend leadership elections.

The decision came after many called to delay the process.

“We’re still discussing. We ran out of time,” Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) told reporters after senators broke up the meeting. They are planning to convene again at 2 p.m. EST to resume discussions.

Johnson on Monday had pledged to walk out of the room if his Republican colleagues proceed with Tuesday elections. GOP Sens. Mike Lee (Utah) and Rick Scott (Fla.) also pushed to postpone.

Senate conservatives have tried to derail Sen. John Thune’s (R-S.D.) bid to serve another term as Republican Senate leader, attempting to leverage how he would lead the lame-duck session to push the last of Trump’s agenda through a Republican-controlled Congress.

Thune told reporters Monday he’ll listen to his colleagues’ demands for delaying the election but indicated he doesn’t see a need to do so.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told CBS News he hoped to see a “different direction.”

“This was the worst set of losses since Watergate, and Watergate was after one of the biggest political scandals in American history,” Hawley said. “I mean, it’s an incredible repudiation to the focus of this Congress over the last two years.”

Meanwhile, in the House : Republicans in the lower chamber have been holding candidate forums this morning, and a final leadership vote is expected for later in the day.

House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) on Monday called for a delay so the GOP can reflect on midterm losses before moving on.

articles.title: How new Democratic trifectas could reshape the 2028 presidential election
articles.summary: A string of Democratic victories in state legislatures has put Electoral College reform in the spotlight ahead of 2028. After Democrats clinched trifectas in Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Arizona and Nevada, activists are eager to pass legislation — the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact — that would require participating states to pledge all their electoral votes to…
articles.body:
A string of Democratic victories in state legislatures has put Electoral College reform in the spotlight ahead of 2028.

After Democrats clinched trifectas in Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Arizona and Nevada, activists are eager to pass legislation — the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact — that would require participating states to pledge all their electoral votes to the winner of the popular vote.

The compact has support from 18 states and Washington, D.C., making up 222 Electoral College votes, and proponents of the compact need states that represent 48 more electoral votes to greenlight the agreement.

But bypassing the Electoral College will be easier said than done as election law experts caution the compact may require approval from Congress and may invite possible litigation should the states charge ahead.

“The whole point is that these compacting states are trying to change the way we run elections, but it also affects essentially how all the noncompacting states participate,” explained Derek Muller, a University of Notre Dame Law School professor who said he believes the move would require congressional approval.

The Electoral College was created by the Founding Fathers as a compromise between those who wanted Congress involved in electing the president and those who preferred that citizens directly elect the president.

The number of Electoral College votes each state receives is based on the number of the state’s congressional districts in addition to one vote for each of its two senators, meaning the smallest states have at least three Electoral College votes.

This system for electing presidents has come under fire in instances where the president didn’t win the popular vote.

Five presidents have won the Electoral College but lost the national vote. President Trump’s 2016 election was the last time this occurred.

Advocates of the national popular vote argue the system does a better job of reflecting what the plurality of the people in the country want.

“As a conservative trapped behind the blue wall of Minnesota — the only state that voted for Walter Mondale — I didn’t feel like my vote counted in presidential elections in my lifetime,” Patrick Rosenstiel, who’s backing efforts to change the presidential electoral system to the national popular vote, told The Hill, referencing former Vice President Walter Mondale’s unsuccessful White House run against former President Reagan in 1984.

“One person, one vote is a foundational principle of American democracy,” he added.

Should Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin pass the interstate compact, it would bring the number of electoral votes in support of the move to 266. Advocates would then only need Arizona or Nevada to sign on to tip over the 270 vote threshold for the compact to theoretically go into effect.

So far, only Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), seen as a likely 2028 contender , and Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley (D) have appeared to express interest in pursuing national popular vote legislation in their states.

Other Democrats have been less clear on where they stand. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) declined to say whether there was support for the interstate compact in the state during a recent interview with AZ Family . Nevada’s Gov.-elect Aaron Ford (D) told The Hill that he is focused on affordability and “there will be a time to talk about presidential elections.”

The office of Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson (D) of Michigan did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. She has not publicly expressed her stance on the issue.

Even if enough states join the interstate compact, experts point to plenty of legal hurdles and logistical challenges that could hinder its implementation.

First, there are questions around whether the interstate compact would require approval from Congress.

The Constitution states : “No State shall, without the Consent of Congress … enter into any Agreement or Compact with another State.” Muller, however, noted the Supreme Court has interpreted that clause to mean that only certain compacts are subject to the requirement.

“A lot of times over the years the court has looked at compacts, even if Congress hasn’t consented, and said, ‘Well, that’s OK. … It doesn’t really affect the balance of power with the federal government. Doesn’t affect other states, so we’re OK with it.’” Muller said.

Muller suggested the current Supreme Court, which places emphasis on adhering to the constitutional text, “is probably going to be more skeptical of those kinds of claims that may have been popular 50 years ago.”

But there are also questions about what the implementation of the compact would mean for states that didn’t sign on to the pledge. Muller used Alabama as a hypothetical. The state has not entered the interstate compact, objecting to awarding its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the national popular vote.

“Alabama, which is not a part of the compact, might look back and say, ‘Wait a minute, you all changed the rules for how we do our presidential elections,’ and we really had no say in that,” he continued. “And so, to me, that is a pretty significant change in power for states that don’t enter into the compact.”

If implemented for 2028, it would introduce unanswered questions about what would happen if a compacting state’s population decreased, reducing its number of Electoral College votes and scrambling the required 270-vote threshold.

Electoral votes are allocated on the basis of the U.S. census, which is conducted every 10 years. If the population of one or more compacting states drops in the 2030 census, it’s unclear whether it would prompt the elimination of the winner-take-all system for the 2032 presidential election.

Some opponents also argue the national vote compact could make campaigning incredibly expensive, as it would force candidates to compete for every vote across the map. And even then, campaigns may decide to prioritize denser areas over more sparsely populated ones.

“They would still slice and dice up the electorate to try to figure out who to talk to, who not to talk to, what to say to which group of people,” Trent England, founder and executive director of Save Our States, told The Hill, adding that the “national popular vote doesn’t take the politics out of politics.”

Rosenstiel, however, argued those hurdles can be overcome. He suggested Congress may not even need to sign off on the interstate compact if enough states sign on, and he asserted the move would not encroach on federal supremacy.

“The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact doesn’t even involve a federal power,” he said.

Rosenstiel also suggested the national popular vote would encourage parties to put their best candidates forward. Presidential hopefuls would have to make the case to more of the electorate in states that regularly take a back seat on the campaign trail.

“It’d probably make campaigning even more expensive because you would have to travel the entire country and campaign everywhere,” Robert Alexander, director of the Bowling Green State University Democracy and Public Policy Network and a political science professor, said.

“But what’s so wrong with campaigning everywhere to be president of the United States?” he quipped.

articles.title: US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds
articles.summary: The report by a Republican-led congressional committee follows a 15-month investigation into the handling of the late disgraced financier's case.
articles.body:
Crimes committed by the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein after 2005 could have been prevented were it not for "failures" by federal investigators and prosecutors, a congressional investigation has concluded.

The Republican-led US House Oversight Committee on Tuesday released its final report into what it described as the "decades-long" mishandling of the criminal investigations into Epstein and his long-term associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The report's findings are based on interviews and depositions with witnesses, government files, and financial records over a 15-month period.

Epstein died in 2019 as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

"While some of these failures involved an exercise in poor judgement by the USAO, others appeared to be the result of Epstein's pervasive and wide-reaching influence," the report reads, referring to the US Attorney's Office.

It states that, rather than fully investigating allegations in other states, the USAO for the Southern District of Florida entered an agreement with Epstein in 2007 allowing him to evade federal prosecution.

'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home

Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison , investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.

Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.

It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.

The DoJ has released millions of pages of Epstein-related files in response to legislation from Congress.

Earlier this year, the department had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.

The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment.

The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors.

"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee.

He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.

The department remains under bipartisan scruntiny regarding the Epstein files.

In the state of New Mexico, where Epstein had a ranch, the top state prosecutor accused the DoJ of stonewalling their criminal investigation.

"With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed," a spokesperson for the department said in response to Comer's report.

"The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."

The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".

Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.

The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.

In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".

Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents".

"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections.

The family members of one of Epstein's most prominent accusers, the late Virginia Roberts Giuffre, thanked Comer for releasing Tuesday's report.

"A sentence from the report stands out to us: 'Questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all its relevant documents.' We could not agree more and urge that all 7 million-plus files be released," Sky and Amanda Roberts said in a statement.

"There are many more individuals who have yet to be identified and brought to justice," they said.

articles.title: Appeals court limits Trump DOJ’s access to journalists’ private chat logs
articles.summary: A federal appeals court’s three-judge panel unanimously limited Tuesday the Trump administration’s broad access to journalists’ LinkedIn records as part of a national security leak investigation, suggesting it could impart a “damaging blow” to First Amendment rights. The ruling, written by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson, a Reagan appointee, stated the Justice Department’s (DOJ) attempt to…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court’s three-judge panel unanimously limited Tuesday the Trump administration’s broad access to journalists’ LinkedIn records as part of a national security leak investigation, suggesting it could impart a “damaging blow” to First Amendment rights.

The ruling, written by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson, a Reagan appointee, stated the Justice Department’s (DOJ) attempt to access reporters’ private message data on the popular networking site could expose sources’ identities and, in turn, hinder future reporting on “governmental behavior of dubious legality and integrity.”

Wilkinson, Biden-appointed Nicole Berner and Andrew Wynn, an Obama appointee, also ruled a district court can narrow the set of records the Trump administration can access. It undercut the DOJ investigation into an unidentified news outlet’s reporting that revealed “a top-secret United States military operation in a foreign country.”

“Press freedom is among those things viewed by autocrats worldwide as a threat to their grip on power,” Wilkinson wrote. “Criminal prosecutions freed from partisanship and retribution, a fearless and independent judicial system, and a secure and accessible electoral process all serve to supplement press freedom in distinguishing liberty from oppression.”

Wilkinson later wrote that, while the judges respect the government’s desire to investigate leaks tied to national security concerns, “respect does not translate into license to round up” journalists’ private information for the purposes of doing so.

“Our review of this order persuades us that, in its present form, it is substantially overbroad,” he wrote.

Trump administration prosecutors asked LinkedIn to supply them with 18 months’ worth of private message data for certain journalists, with the also DOJ obtaining an order from U.S. District Judge Elizabeth Hanes forbade the platform from informing the reporters of such request.

LinkedIn challenged the order, stating it would impact its ability to communicate with its users. Wilkinson wrote that, while the order might “catch sources relevant to the government’s investigation,” it would also unveil confidential sources.

“The targeted journalists reported on almost 1,000 stories on a wide range of issues during the relevant period and investigated an unknown number of others never published,” he continued. “Many of those stories appear far removed from the Article that the leak at least partially enabled.”

The Trump administration has sought to limit some news outlets from covering the White House, briefly restricting CNN, Politico and MS NOW’s ability to report on grounds before a judge extended an order allowing them to cover the president. Though the administration has continued to bar CNN from performing its television press pool duties in certain areas of the campus and on Air Force One.

President Trump himself has frequently quarreled with reporters during his second term, asserting during an Ohio rally last month reporters from The New York Times and other media outlets should be “arrested .”

articles.title: Liberal podcasters tell TPUSA to ‘f--- off’ as Charlie Kirk backlash costs them advertisers
articles.summary: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan of the “I’ve Had It" podcast apologized for laughing at a joke about Kirk’s body, but soon doubled down on TPUSA as advertisers cut ties.
articles.body: A source in the office of a prominent nationally elected Democrat called "I've Had It" podcast host Jennifer Welch a "sicko" after she allegedly sought help managing backlash over a joke about digging up Charlie Kirk's body. Welch denied the source's account as she and co-host Angie Sullivan renewed their attacks on Turning Point USA , with Sullivan telling the conservative organization to "f--- all the way off" despite the hosts' earlier apology. The controversy has also cost the podcast advertisers. Cash App announced it was ending its sponsorship, saying on social media: "We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast." Luxury bedding company Boll and Branch also reportedly dropped its sponsorship, while Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet claimed on X that several other advertisers had withdrawn their support. The hosts apologized over the weekend, but Sullivan subsequently told TPUSA to "f--- off" while Welch said her apology was motivated by her own convictions rather than pressure from the conservative organization. "Alright there's a huge online, cancellation campaign from all the titty babies over at Turning Point who want the 'I've Had It' podcast canceled," Welch said in a video posted to the podcast's YouTube channel. She accused Turning Point USA of "spearheading" the campaign because they're "losers and they lost" and "want to prove to their donors we can cancel libs." SOCIAL MEDIA HORRIFIED BY DAVE CHAPPELLE’S SICK ‘JOKE’ ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK’S MURDER "When we apologize for laughing at a joke on our podcast, that wasn't for you. That was for us," Welch continued. "Because someone I loved very much died from gun violence two years ago, and I just didn't feel good about that. And that apology was so that when I advocate for commonsense gun reform that I'm doing it clean and clear. I don't expect you to understand this because at Turning Point y'all laugh at violence all the time." FAR-LEFT PODCASTER CALLS FOR 'PISTOLS FIRING' TOWARD JD VANCE, DEFEATING HIM IN 2028 A Democratic source told Fox News Digital that Welch called them while seeking advice on how to manage the fallout from her comments. According to the source, Welch blamed Turning Point USA for the controversy rather than expressing remorse. "I am not Turning Point. I'm a national Dem and we don't need people like her in this party because it is exactly what we don’t like about the hard right," the source said. The source also called Welch a "sicko" and estimated that the podcast had lost "tens of thousands" of dollars in sponsorships over the weekend. The source further alleged that Welch's team used ChatGPT to help formulate a response to the controversy and identify "ways out of this." Welch denied the claims in a text message to Fox News Digital, saying she had not spoken with a top Democrat and that the podcast had not used ChatGPT. "Those are both wholly untrue," she said. A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH "We laughed at an insensitive joke. We regret it, and we apologized," Welch said. She added that the podcast had removed the segment and donated to Everytown for Gun Safety, a gun-control advocacy organization. "Turning Point, the group leading the cancellation against us, mocks violence and never apologizes," Welch added. "We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren’t going anywhere." While discussing their apology, Welch called TPUSA a "hateful organization," and Sullivan said she was "not going to be lectured by these people." "These people support representatives to Congress that protect pedophiles and sex traffickers. They're completely fine with American citizens being gunned down on the streets of Minnesota. They're fine with putting people in cages and treating them like animals," she continued. "And for those of you at Turning Point who are worried that I don't talk enough, but yet, you don't believe in universal human rights, I want you to hear me: F--- off. F--- all the way off." TURNING POINT USA TURNS THE TABLES ON 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' AFTER LATE-NIGHT SKETCH MOCKS CAMPUS RECRUITERS The controversy began during an episode last week in which Welch and Sullivan read social media posts celebrating Democratic victories in the midterm elections. Both laughed after Welch read one post saying, "We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." The hosts also suggested, without presenting evidence, that Kirk's accused killer supported President Donald Trump. Voter records, however, showed that he was unaffiliated and had not voted in the previous two general elections. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER After the episode sparked backlash, Welch and Sullivan posted an apology Saturday saying they had laughed at an "insensitive joke" and "should not have laughed." They said there was "nothing funny about gun violence." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The hosts' remarks also drew criticism from Democrats, including strategist Kaivan Shroff. "They are not helping Democrats," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "They are hijacking the attention Democrats actually earned at the ballot box."

articles.title: House Oversight Republicans release final Epstein report
articles.summary: The GOP’s report says President Donald Trump was not implicated in Epstein’s trafficking of women and young girls.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Republicans on the House Oversight Committee released their full report Tuesday on Jeffrey Epstein, ending their monthslong investigation but providing few new details on the convicted sex offender .

The report was released with little fanfare after two headline-generating years of investigative work, dropped as House Republicans hold elections to select new leaders. The probe brought in numerous allies on the disgraced financier, as well as high profile Trump administration officials.

The GOP’s report claims President Trump was not implicated in Epstein’s trafficking of women and young girls and accuses law enforcement and federal prosecutors of repeated failures, allowing Epstein’s abuse to continue long after his criminal investigation in 2005.

“The evidence we uncovered makes clear that the Department of Justice must interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records,” it states.

The panel also concluded that many of Epstein’s closest associates were unaware of his activities — a detail that caught the attention of Democrats.

“The Committee’s investigation instead tends to show that the willful ignorance of those in Epstein’s orbit enabled him to continue his offenses for so many years,” Republicans wrote in the 137-page report.

Democrats on the panel blasted what they deemed an incomplete report on the investigation — one they have vowed to continue as they take control of Congress next year.

“Oversight Republicans have released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, said in a statement. “The Department of Justice continues to illegally withhold over 2.5 million pages of documents, there’s been no investigation of Ghislaine Maxwell’s transfer, and Attorney General Todd Blanche has yet to testify about his role in the largest government cover-up of the modern era.”

“We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation. We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump,” he added. “Our work is just getting started.”

Departing Chair Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) called for additional legislation on the Epstein files in a statement.

“Congress must also pass legislation protecting the ability of individuals with knowledge of sexual abuse and survivors to speak freely about these crimes, regardless of nondisclosure agreements. We cannot undo the horrific harm inflicted on these women,” he wrote, in part.

Among those interviewed during the probe were former President Clinton, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

Reps. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) have floated a second bill to follow their Epstein Files Transparency Act — which ordered the Justice Department to release its files on the case — that would make it easier for state-level prosecutors to bring charges.

articles.title: Warnock ducks questions about backing Schumer as Senate majority leader
articles.summary: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) isn’t committing to backing Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, repeatedly dodging questions about whether he’d support the New York Democrat in a leadership election. The lawmaker appeared on “The Breakfast Club” on Monday and declined multiple times to directly answer questions from the nationally syndicated radio show’s co-host, Charlamagne…
articles.body:
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) isn’t committing to backing Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, repeatedly dodging questions about whether he’d support the New York Democrat in a leadership election.

The lawmaker appeared on “ The Breakfast Club ” on Monday and declined multiple times to directly answer questions from the nationally syndicated radio show’s co-host, Charlamagne tha God, about Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.).

“There are so many people” calling for Schumer and Jeffries “to step aside or to fundamentally change how they lead,” Charlamagne, who was born Lenard McKelvey, told Warnock.

“Do you believe Democratic leadership understands what voters were demanding in this election?” he asked.

“I spent a lot of time on the ground listening. I campaigned in about 10 states trying to help us with the Senate majority,” Warnock said, adding that Americans are “deeply frustrated” and “hungry.”

“But does Democratic leadership understand that?” Charlamagne asked, mentioning Schumer and Jeffries again.

“I think that’s a conversation we need to have, and we will continue to have inside the caucus,” Warnock replied.

“In terms of leadership, I’m open to hearing whoever in the caucus thinks that they should lead in this moment,” he added.

“I want to hear that vision, but it’s got to center the concerns of ordinary people — it can’t be about Beltway politics. It’s about how we actually deliver to the people,” Warnock said.

“But does the party need new leadership, or does it need a new agenda under the same?” Charlamagne asked.

“I think the whole country needs a new agenda,” Warnock said, before calling President Trump the “most corrupt president we’ve had in American history” and a “vile human being.”

“The Trump era is indicative of the brokenness and the deep pain that people are feeling in our country, and I think we need leaders who are going to take on the corruption,” he continued.

Schumer has expressed confidence he’ll be reelected as Senate majority leader next month despite some incoming Democratic lawmakers, including Sens.-elect Annie Andrews (S.C.), Adam Hamilton (Kan.), Abdul El-Sayed (Mich.) and Troy Jackson (Maine), saying they would not back him.

“The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader. But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want,” Schumer said earlier this month.

Following the massive wins by Democrats in the midterm elections, a progressive group called Indivisible urged lawmakers to replace Schumer as the leader in the upper chamber, calling for a “new generation of Democratic fighters.”

Pressed again later in the interview by Charlamagne on whether Schumer “is the right person to lead this new Democratic Senate majority,” Warnock responded, “I think we need fresh vision, fresh ideas, and I’m open to hearing whoever thinks they have that.”

“Do you think he is the person?” Charlamagne asked, referring to Schumer.

“The process for choosing the leader will come up soon enough, and I’ll be engaged with that. But right now, I’m focused on delivering, and I will not tolerate any leader that’s not going to take on this corruption.”

During the “Breakfast Club” interview, Charlamagne asked Warnock about the historic gains for Democrats on Election Day.

“When you look at the results, what do you believe the American people were voting for? Were they voting for Democrats? Were they voting against Trump? Or were they just voting for a fundamentally different kind of politics?” he asked.

“All of this corruption, healthcare that they can’t afford. People are just feeling crushed,” Warnock said.

“It definitely was a complete rebuke of the last 10 years of MAGA,” Charlamagne said, referring to Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.

“But I don’t want Democrats to get comfortable and think that they actually went out there and voted because they trust the Democratic Party,” Charlamagne told the lawmaker.

“I agree with that. I think both political parties don’t have a good brand right now,” Warnock said.

“And I think there’s a way in which people have been trying for a long time almost to get above politics.”

“I do think both parties are very much on trial right now, and people want to know who will deliver for everyday people,” Warnock said, “which is the work that I try to do every single day.”

articles.title: Democrats rally behind GOP lawmaker's Hegseth impeachment push, signal more to come in January
articles.summary: Democrats rallied behind Rep. Thomas Massie's eight-count impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth, citing the Iran war and Nicolás Maduro's capture.
articles.body: Top Democrats are lining up behind Republican Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth, signaling that the fight could continue when Democrats take control of Congress in January. "Hard yes on the Hegseth impeachment resolution," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said ahead of its introduction. The Democratic reactions online telegraph an appetite to scrutinize Trump’s administration through congressional power once their majorities are formally sworn in in January, at the start of the 120th Congress. HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE Massie himself framed the effort as likely to be repeated in the new year. "My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dems control Congress," Massie said. Already, Rep. Al Green, D-Texas — who has repeatedly introduced impeachment resolutions against President Donald Trump — urged his colleagues to expand their horizons for impeachment moments after Massie introduced his resolution. "If the Constitution is to be honored and Congress respected, a president whom many members of Congress have declared impeachable must be impeached. Failure to do so would be another step toward making the Constitution meaningless and Congress powerless," Green wrote online. Massie is filing eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution in Iran and Yemen, failing to prevent civilian casualties, using lethal force in an extrajudicial manner, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a sovereign foreign leader without congressional authorization with the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Although he didn’t mention Massie by name, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed Jeffries’ enthusiasm. "The Senate needs to put Pete Hegseth on trial so we can remove him for his catastrophic failure in Iran," Schumer said in remarks on the Senate floor. Even beyond a review of Hegseth’s record as war secretary, some Democrats argued that removing Hegseth would help end the conflict — a war that Democrats believe has extended far beyond Trump’s power to use the military in a conflict without a declaration of war from Congress. "Impeach Hegseth. End the war," Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., said in a post to X. 7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS Calls for Hegseth’s impeachment have circulated among Democrats for months. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has frequently called for Hegseth to step down. "It’s way past time," Omar, who shares her home state of Minnesota with Hegseth, said in September. "He has made a mockery of our country; it risks our national security and it’s losing us respect." On Monday afternoon, Omar doubled down on those calls, arguing that Hegseth had operated beyond the boundaries of his office in conducting strikes on boats off the coast of Venezuela for allegedly carrying narcotics. "Pete Hegseth has grossly abused his position as Secretary of Defense. He is waging an illegal war in Iran, conducting extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and continues to put innocent civilians in harm’s way," Omar said. Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, echoed Omar’s list of grievances. "He has caused the military and the members therein to have the lowest morale we’ve seen by his actions — firing individuals just based upon just cultural issues, basically. That kind of thing is not who we want to be a representative of us in the United States defense, and I think he should resign. And if I have to vote on it, whether it’s today or tomorrow or next week, to say that he should be impeached, I will vote so," Meeks said on Tuesday. When asked if Democrats should renew the effort in January should Massie’s resolution face defeat, Meeks hinted that he believed so. "We’re going to continue to dig into him, his involvement, his advice that led us to this illegal war in the first place." The House must approve articles of impeachment, and the Senate must vote to convict Hegseth for him to be removed from office. The resolution can clear the House with a simple majority but requires two-thirds of senators to affirm a guilty verdict.

articles.title: Moore on Stephen Miller: ‘I will work with anybody. I will bow to nobody’
articles.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Tuesday expressed a willingness to work with new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. “Listen, I always respect a president’s decision — or an executive decision — to have a chief of staff who they want as their chief of staff,” Moore said at the U.S. Chamber of…
articles.body:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Tuesday expressed a willingness to work with new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

“Listen, I always respect a president’s decision — or an executive decision — to have a chief of staff who they want as their chief of staff,” Moore said at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s B20 USA 2026 event when asked about collaborating with the new chief of staff.

“It is not lost on me at all that Stephen Miller is the architect of some of the most racist, xenophobic, homophobic policies that we have in the United States of America,” he added. “And I think we have to be honest about that. But, you know, one thing I’ve always said to the people of my state is I will work with anybody. I will bow to nobody.”

Last week , President Trump announced that his then-chief of staff Susie Wiles was exiting the White House and Miller, a longtime adviser, would take up her role.

Miller’s promotion followed Republicans’ blowout loss in this year’s 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats poised to take the House and Senate next year.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Most Democrats have decried Miller’s stances on immigration enforcement. The new chief of staff is a hardliner when it comes to immigration and is seen as the architect behind the Trump administration’s mass deportation efforts.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Anti-Israel socialist silent on Jewish business boycott in district he's set to represent
articles.summary: Christopher Rabb, a democratic socialist elected in the Blue Wave, stayed silent as Democrats condemned a Jewish business boycott in Philadelphia.
articles.body: A newly elected Democratic socialist congressman from Philadelphia did not respond to questions about a boycott targeting Jewish-owned businesses in the city, even as prominent Pennsylvania Democrats condemned the demonstration, which coincided with the anniversary of Kristallnacht. Rep.-elect Christopher Rabb, D-Pa., who currently represents part of Northwest Philadelphia in the state House, did not respond to requests for comment about the boycott, which drew a large counterprotest supporting Jewish residents and businesses in Rittenhouse Square. A staff member at Rabb's Harrisburg office acknowledged Fox News Digital's inquiry and the two-hour deadline for a response. Fox News Digital also contacted Rabb's Harrisburg and campaign offices by email. TENSIONS FLARE AS DEMONSTRATORS TARGET JEWISH RESTAURANTS, DRAWING MASSIVE COUNTERPROTEST Over the weekend, the left-wing cycling group Philly Bike on Your Left helped organize a boycott targeting Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square neighborhood. Flyers promoting the rally carried the slogans "No business for Zionists" and "Not in our city," according to published reports. Philly Bike on Your Left could not immediately be reached for comment. Kristallnacht, or the Night of Broken Glass, refers to the November 1938 Nazi-organized attacks on Jews, synagogues and Jewish-owned businesses across Germany and Austria. DSA ACCUSED OF ‘ELEVATING’ ANTISEMITIC, PRO-TERROR RHETORIC AFTER HASAN PIKER HOSTS ELECTION STREAM Rabb has been an outspoken critic of Israel. He previously declared that the "Nakba never ended" — a reference to the displacement of Palestinians during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war — and has appeared with anti-Israel streamer Hasan Piker. Rabb has also called for Pennsylvania and the federal government to divest from Israel and participated in "war criminal" protests against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu outside the United Nations. Rabb's lack of response contrasted with public condemnations from several prominent Pennsylvania Democrats, including Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is Jewish, Philadelphia City Council President Kenyatta Johnson and Sen. John Fetterman. Rabb currently represents part of Northwest Philadelphia in the state legislature but is set to represent a much larger portion of the city in Congress, including Center City and Rittenhouse Square, where the boycott took place. Fox News Digital asked Rabb whether he supports the boycott's objectives, whether Jewish-owned businesses should be targeted over the Israeli government's actions and whether he agrees with fellow Democrats who condemned the demonstration, including progressive Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner. Krasner noted the boycott's proximity to the anniversary of Kristallnacht and described the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel as a "terrorist attack". He also emphasized that "there is a difference between the leadership of a country and the people who reside there." He drew a comparison between criticism of Netanyahu and opposition to President Donald Trump, arguing that people should not be held responsible for the actions of their political leaders. "Donald Trump didn't do so well in this last election. Are all Americans the same as Donald Trump? Can they all be blamed for the things that he has done — is that fair?" he said, adding that legitimate demonstrations should not include epithets such as "ZioBusiness" — language he compared to rhetoric used by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke. Although the boycott drew support from socialist activists, the Philadelphia chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America denied organizing or endorsing the demonstration, telling Fox News Digital that the group had no official involvement. The group nevertheless criticized Shapiro, Johnson and Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., accusing them of participating in a "chorus of bad-faith and dangerous conflation of antisemitism with anti-Zionism and invoking comparisons of Kristallnacht that trivialize trauma and suppress political speech." GAZA-BORN DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST LAUNCHES PRIMARY BID AGAINST SEN JOHN FETTERMAN "Democratic voters sent a resounding message to a Trump administration engaged in violent acts of war abroad and at home… Yet in the wake of these historic victories, establishment Democrats have retreated to the very playbook that cost them the election in 2024." Boyle publicly condemned the planned boycott Thursday, issuing a statement condemning the plans as anti-Semitism . "[T]argeting local businesses simply because they are Jewish-owned is simply wrong. Indeed, it is antisemitism," Boyle said. "It evokes the darkest chapters of history, including the Nazi boycotts of Jewish businesses in the 1930s and Kristallnacht." articles.title: Jim Jordan becomes new House GOP leader after closed-door vote, defeating Steve Scalise
articles.summary: Jim Jordan defeated Steve Scalise in a narrow secret ballot to become House GOP minority leader and President Trump's top defender in Congress.
articles.body: House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, will be President Donald Trump's top defender in Congress next year after winning a closed-door election for minority leader on Tuesday, sources told Fox News Digital. Jordan defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., currently the House of Representatives' No. 2 leader, in what's believed to be a narrow race. Jordan received 106 votes to Scalise’s 73, sources in the room told Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital heard loud, sustained applause from outside in the hallway when Jordan’s win became official. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., also handily defeated Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, for the No. 2 leadership job of minority whip. The final vote count was 103 to 76, per sources. Sources said House GOP Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain, R-Mich., meanwhile, also survived a challenge and kept her job. JORDAN EMERGES AS POTENTIAL NEXT GOP LEADER IF DEMS SEIZE HOUSE Republicans huddled for a candidate forum on Tuesday morning where all GOP lawmakers running for leadership positions were peppered with questions by their colleagues. Sources inside the room for their Tuesday morning leadership forum said Scalise and Jordan both pitched themselves as the best person to unify the conference, but also signaled they would give a wide berth for lawmakers to "vote their districts," as one person put it. The question-and-answer session for House Republicans before electing their leader was largely cordial, Fox News Digital was told. Several people inquired about how both prospective leaders would unify the conference after their midterm losses and how they would handle leaks to journalists, Fox News Digital was told. Jordan himself told Fox News Digital he believed the forum went well but declined to go further, stating he does not divulge details of closed-door meetings. The voting body consisted of incumbent House Republicans and GOP members-elect who are projected to win their races from last week's midterms. Votes were cast via secret ballot, meaning none of those in the room had to reveal who they chose. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI And the results on Tuesday show the House GOP was hungry for change. Jordan's victory comes fresh off the back of a historic loss for Republicans across both state and federal races. The magnitude of the losses forced Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to announce he was stepping aside and not seeking another leadership position for the next two years. "I personally like Steve, but he's been in leadership since before I was in Congress. And Jim Jordan, while he's a leader in Congress, he hasn't been part of the leadership team. He basically rose through the ranks because he was super effective," Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald, R-Wis., another Jordan ally, told Fox News Digital the Ohio Republican "understands what we're up against," adding, "His ability to communicate is really kind of unrivaled by anybody else in the House right now." Jordan has long been among the House GOP's brightest stars, rapidly gaining influence over the last decade as one of Trump's most vocal supporters in Washington. articles.title: Trump administration seeks to cut food aid for more than six million people
articles.summary: Trump’s proposal builds on earlier cuts to federal food aid programme used by more than 36 million low-income Americans.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has proposed new eligibility requirements for the country’s largest food aid programme that would see some 6.3 million people removed from it.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) published a proposed rule (PDF) on Tuesday that would end automatic eligibility in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), doing away with current provisions that automatically make households eligible for the programme if they meet state-administered requirements for another programme, called Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).

“These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility’s statutory purpose of simplifying program administration,” the agency said in the proposal, which will be open to public comments for 30 days.

More than 36 million people are currently enrolled in SNAP, which is the largest federal food aid programme for low-income families. An individual in the programme receives an average of about $190 each month, while a household receives an average monthly benefit of $356 in groceries.

The SNAP programme itself requires that households earn less than 130 percent of the federal government’s poverty level to qualify. Currently, households that qualify for the TANF programme – which has requirements that vary by state and can accommodate households earning up to 200 percent of the federal poverty level – are also automatically eligible for SNAP.

According to the USDA, the proposed changes would remove about 17 percent of SNAP beneficiaries from the programme, some 6.3 million people. The cuts would also have other one-off effects, including removing 1.8 million children from a federal programme providing them with free school lunches, because they would no longer qualify for the SNAP programme.

Democratic lawmakers have criticised the Republican administration’s attempt to cut the federal food aid programme.

“The proposed rule would make it harder to ‌meet ‌basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs,” Minnesota Democratic Representative ‌Angie Craig said in a statement on Monday.

“SNAP is a highly effective and efficient program when it is allowed to work as designed,” Craig’s statement continued. “Unfortunately, the Trump administration and the outgoing Republican majority in Congress have undermined the program’s integrity at every turn, harming millions of vulnerable Americans in the process.”

Democratic Senator Cory Booker from New Jersey called the proposal “despicable” in a social media post on Monday.

“Trump is set to kick millions more people off of SNAP, when Americans are already struggling with grocery prices. It is despicable. We need to be helping people afford groceries, not deepening cuts to the safety net that keeps families from going hungry,” Booker said.

Builds on previous Trump moves targeting food aid

The new cuts build on previous changes to the SNAP programme by the Trump administration, which has said many of those receiving aid through the federal government are not in need of it.

Some 5.5 million people lost access to SNAP benefits under Trump already, due to changes mandated by the July 2025 Big Beautiful Bill . The legislation expanded work requirements for beneficiaries and made certain categories of immigrants ineligible for the aid. States struggled with new administrative changes and with covering additional costs the federal government passed on to them under the bill.

Then, in November 2025, Trump briefly withheld funding for the SNAP programme entirely, using it as leverage to force Democrats to agree to passing a federal budget. The Democrats refused, and as a result, the federal government was shut down for more than a month. Towards the end of that impasse, Trump refused to use emergency funds to cover the SNAP programme.

At the time, Trump said the administration of former President Joe Biden had been responsible for burdening the government with “billions of billions” of dollars in more spending because of the programme. The benefits, Trump claimed in a Truth Social post without evidence, had been “haphazardly ‘handed’ to anyone for the asking, as opposed to just those in need, which is the purpose of SNAP!”

The Supreme Court eventually struck down lower court rulings, saying Trump could not legally withhold the funding for SNAP, just as lawmakers in Congress reached an agreement to pass a new federal budget and reopen the government.

The Trump administration has continued to push for changes to SNAP.

In December 2025, the administration threatened to withhold funding for the programme from 21 states that refused to hand over data on beneficiaries to the federal government, which the administration said it needed to examine in order to cut fraud.

The new proposal is now open for public comment for the next 30 days.

articles.title: Democrats accused of 'No Kings' hypocrisy over push to change voter-approved trans sports measures
articles.summary: Colorado's Philip Weiser and Rep. Pramila Jayapal face "No Kings" hypocrisy claims after signaling efforts to overturn transgender sports ballot measures.
articles.body: Voters in two Democratic strongholds approved restrictions on transgender participation in girls' sports last week, delivering rare Republican victories amid a blue wave. But Democratic officials are already discussing ways to change the measures, drawing accusations of hypocrisy from Republicans who point to their support for the "No Kings" movement. Colorado Gov.-elect Philip Weiser, who also criticized a separate ballot measure restricting gender-related surgeries for minors, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal , D-Wash., both raised objections to the measures approved in their respective states. At his first post-election news conference, he suggested Colorado's Democratic-controlled legislature could revisit the voter-approved measures, saying that it is "statutory … and a natural and I believe appropriate role for the legislature to say ‘what are the adjustments that need to be added." PRO-TRANS ACTIVISTS HOLD RALLY AGAINST WASHINGTON STATE BALLOT INITIATIVE TO PROTECT GIRLS SPORTS Colorado voters approved ballot measures increasing penalties for fentanyl-related offenses, restricting transgender athletes from competing in sports designated for the opposite biological sex and prohibiting gender-related surgeries for minors. The measures passed even as Democrats swept into power across the state. "I don’t believe it would be acceptable to Colorado to have every student athlete to have to go through full-body examinations or other invasions of privacy," Weiser added of the sports-related referendum, according to the Denver Post. COLORADO MOM WHO SAID DAUGHTER WAS SECRETLY TRANSITIONED HELPS LEAD EFFORT TO BAN BOYS IN GIRLS' SPORTS Weiser did not respond to a request for comment. Republicans in suburban Denver criticized the governor-elect, dubbing him "King Phil I" and characterizing his response as "know[ing] better than Colorado voters in a healthy democracy." "But before the ink on the ballots is even dry, Governor-elect Phil Weiser is already signaling that the vote of the people is merely a ‘suggestion’. With Coloradans approving ballot measures to crack down on fentanyl and protect youth sports and children, Weiser walked up to the podium on Wednesday and essentially declared that the will of the majority needs to pass his personal vibe check first," the Adams County Republican Party said in a statement. Republicans characterized Weiser’s position as "you voted for it, but I don’t like it…" "No Kings," the Adams Republicans added, invoking the protest movement that Weiser has supported through participation in "No Kings" protests. The movement's demonstrations have criticized President Donald Trump over what organizers characterize as authoritarian conduct. The Colorado House Republican caucus echoed the sentiment, adding in a statement: "If the Democrats truly believe there should be ‘No Kings’ in America, it is time they take their own advice." 'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS Meanwhile, in Washington State, Jayapal condemned a similar measure approved by voters. Initiative 638 prohibits students defined as "biologically male" from competing in girls' K-12 school sports and requires students seeking to participate on girls' teams to provide verification of their biological sex from a health care provider. The measure passed with approximately 56% support in the reliably Democratic state. Following the election results, multiple local news outlets reported that Jayapal pledged to "take our state back" after voters approved the initiative. "We're going to start planning for how we overturn these bad initiatives and how we go back to loving everyone with gender inclusivity the way we have for decades," she said, according to several reports. Jayapal did not respond to a request for comment. Critics also pointed to Jayapal's past support for "No Kings" protests, accusing her of contradicting her own rhetoric about respecting the will of voters. One critic highlighted a November 2025 social media post in which Jayapal wrote: "We have democracy for a reason. America doesn’t belong to kings it belongs to the people and we're going to keep it that way." "Rep. Jayapal, this you?" they asked. Jayapal also faced previous criticism over her support for the "No Kings" movement after praising remarks by Britain's King Charles III during his visit to the United States. Washington Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad signaled support for a legal challenge, calling the ballot measure "unconstitutional on its face" and indicating the party would "support [for] organizations planning to challenge it in court." After two years, the legislature can amend or repeal the measure with a simple majority.
